speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 40, respecting visiting forces of His Majesty, and the exercise of command, discipline and attachments of commonwealth forces when serving together.
He said: I do not know that it is necessary to add anything to what is indicated by the notes that accompany the bill. Shortly put, the matters mentioned in the bill were vested in the Imperial parliament under the authority of the Army Act, with the passing of the statute of Westminster the responsibility rested with the dominions, and the various dominions that constitute the British commonwealth of nations have agreed upon a bill, with such changes as local conditions necessitate, and that is bill number 40, the second reading of which I now move. If there are any matters requiring explanation such explanations will be furnished during its progress through the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I accept the statement of the Prime Minister that this bill is necessary as a consequence of the statute of Westminster, and that its purpose is to facilitate training and cooperation as between different forces

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Visiting forces.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, of the
several nations of the British commonwealth of nations. The provisions of the bill however refer to service of these forces together. I shall ask the Prime Minister, when we get into committee, whether it is clearly understood that this service relates only to service together in cooperation for training purposes, not service together in time of war. I am not sure that the bill is not capable of the interpretation of also relating to possible service together in time of war, if, indeed, that is not exactly what is intended.
I assume that the provisions of the bill are all subject to the provisions of existing statutes which govern the placing of the Canadian forces at the disposal of His Majesty outside of Canada, whether it be the army, air forces or naval service, and that the bill as presented is in no way intended to override the fundamental provisions of those acts.
There is just one other point that I should like to mention. The use of the words or rather the designation, "commonwealth forces"
js a new one. The Prime Minister explained at the time of the introduction of the bill that it means the forces belonging to the nations of the British commonwealth. So long as it is understood in that way I take no exception to it, but I should not like it to be assumed that in adopting that term, we are creating under commonwealth forces so-called some new form of Imperial forces, some consolidated or centralized forces.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Tummon in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Definitions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the right hon.
gentleman will see that the definition of "the commonwealth" meets his difficulty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:

Sections 3, 4 and 5 agreed to.
On section 6-Application of section.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This section
applies to the forces of all the dominions and of the United Kingdom. Paragraph (ii) of subsection (2) reads:
(ii) subject to anything to the contrary in the conditions applicable to his service, may place any member of a home force at the disposal of the service authorities of another part of the commonwealth for the purpose of being attached temporarily by those authorities to a force to which this section applies belonging to that part of the commonwealth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: To which the other force belongs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend explain whether under that section, assuming, for example, that another portion of the empire were engaged in war, it would be possible for the Minister of National Defence of Canada to place at the disposition of the forces of that part of the empire members of the Canadian forces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is not what the
section contemplates. I think the explanatory note that is opposite the section is a fair statement of the situation. The explanatory note reads:
This section deals with the attachment of personnel and mutual powers of command. The cooperation in defence matters which has existed now for many years involves the interchange of officers and men, and it is necessary to enable such officers and men to carry on their duties on the same basis as if they were members of the forces to which they are attached. Subsection 4 deals with combined operations and makes it legally possible to have
Visiting Commonwealth Forces

a single command, subject, of course, to the consent of the governments of the component forces.
There is in the bill, so far as I have been able to understand it, nothing that in any way impinges upon the provisions of any existing act of parliament, but owing to the Army Act being no longer applicable this bill makes provision for those matters that were heretofore dealt with by the Army Act. As I say, there is no derogation from the powers of parliament nor any interference with the most complete autonomy and control by our own parliament and country. That is my understanding.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend regard the section as having application in time of war or only in time of peace?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My understanding of it
is that it has no war application, because the question of war, with respect to our forces, is a matter that ultimately has to be determined by this parliament. This legislation is entirely subject to any existing statutes or any that may be passed. It deals with visiting forces or with those that technically are perhaps not visiting forces, that is forces that go from one country to another for the purpose of training. For instance, at various times we have officers attached to the forces of Great Britain, and, as the right hon. gentleman knows, it has been customary for many years to have the same interchange with respect to other parts of the empire. According to my understanding and reading of the measure, it does not apply to a war condition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am glad to have my right hon. friend give that interpretation. Just to make doubly sure of the point which has been mentioned, may I direct his attention to thte concluding sentence of the explanatory note regarding section 6, which reads as follows:
Subsection 4 deals with combined operations and makes it legally possible to have a single command, subject, of course, to the consent of the governments of the component forces.
The Prime Minister has emphasized the importance of the control of parliament in time of war, but if the provisions of this act were to apply to service in time of war, it would give to the government of the day, in view of that explanatory note, the power which I think, and which I believe my right hon. friend thinks, ought to belong to parliament. In other words, the government of the country apart from express authority from parliament should not have the authority to place Cana-

dian forces under a single command in any other part of the empire or in any other part of the world.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The former Minister of National Defence is familiar with the necessity for this legislation. I am not a military man. The necessity arises out of the Imperial conference of 1926 and the subsequent steps taken in 1930. The bill as I understand it was agreed to by the representatives of the various countries. The preamble makes it abundantly clear. It says:
Whereas it is expedient to make provision with respect to forces of His Majesty from other parts of the British commonwealth or from a colony when visiting the Dominion of Canada; and with respect to the exercise of command and discipline when forces of His Majesty from different parts of the commonwealth are serving together; and with respect to the attachment of members of one such force to another such force, and with respect to deserters from such forces:
It might well be that if parliament had taken action as required by existing statutes, "serving together" might be in time of war. That is clear, is it not?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is what I think it does mean myself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But I think it is clear that there is no interference with the power of parliament. The words in the explanatory note, "the consent of the governments of the component forces," mean in that instance the consent that is provided for by the statutes of this country which lay down the only method by which forces can be dispatched out of this country, which is of course with the consent of this parliament. If another country permits its foTces to come here and our forces are serving with those of another country, then section 4 provides that any member of the other force-we will say it is an Australian force that is serving together with the Canadian force-shall be treated and shall have the like powers of command over the home force as if he were a member of the home force of relative rank. That is, if you have the tjvo forces serving together here and commanded by an officer from, say, South Africa or Australia, he should have the same powers as though he were dealing with his home farces.

If this
applies merely to forces on a visit for purposes of training, why is subsection 4 inserted?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Subsection 4 deals with
unity of command, and undoubtedly under certain circumstances would apply in time of

Visiting Commonwealth Forces
war. But no force can leave this country except with the consent of this parliament. That is clear under our own statutes.

My right
hon. friend did not get my point. If the act is merely for the purpose of controlling visiting forces-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It goes further than
that. I stated a moment ago that it goes further than that with respect to matters of discipline, desertion, and matters of that kind. It goes further also with respect to unity of command where two forces are serving together, and the position which is occupied by whoever may be in command is made equivalent to the position he would have if he was serving with his home forces in his home country. But this legislation gives no power in any sense to alter the provisions of existing legislation with respect to the movement of armed forces from this country. That can only be done, as I understand the law, with the consent of parliament.

My point
is that if this act is merely for the purpose of governing existing forces-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I say it is more than
that.

-then in
case of war, if parliament takes action and sends forces from Canada, those forces will be under the command of a superior officer in Great Britain or from some other part of the empire, and it will mean that we shall be passing control of our army into their hands.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On the contrary, they
might be passing control into our hands. It does not touch the substance or principles which have to do with peace and war and the movement of forces. But when a home force and another force to which this section applies are serving together, then any member of the other force shall be treated and shall have over members of the home force the like powers of command as if he were a member of the home force of relative rank. That is, if forces from New Zealand and Canada were serving together, and a New Zealander were in command of the two forces, he would have the same position as one of his rank would have if he were a Canadian in charge of the two forces. That is all. It is merely for the purpose of establishing, just as the section says, some cooperation in defence matters; and if reliance is placed upon cooperation, then there should be no conflict in case of two forces, one from New Zealand 53719-173
and one from Canada, serving together as to whether a Canadian of a given rank was in command or a New Zealander of the same rank. But if a New Zealander were in control of the two forces he should have the same powers of command over the forces as though he were a Canadian; and vice versa, if a Canadian were in command of Australian and Canadian forces serving together, he should have the same rank as he would have if he were an Australian of that rank under their statute.
The reason I am speaking with very great care about the matter is because it is not a matter about which I have any technical knowledge. I am only speaking by the book, as I understand it. The discussion that took place in the conference of 1930 is summarized by the note that appears on page 2 of the bill. As a result of that, discussions took place for the purpose of trying to draw up a bill that would not by any possible chance be considered as impinging upon the power of parliament or upon the strength of existing statutes that dealt with substantive matters of military defence. I think that that is a correct statement of the position.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I feel sure that the assurance which the Prime Minister is giving the house is one which he believes to be absolutely correct, and one which certainly we are all glad to have. At the same time, I do think that the wording of the statute itself would seem to give, on occasions at least, some powers to the Minister of National Defence himself, and on other occasions to the governor in council itself which we have not up to the present assumed would be existing in relation to or in time of war. May I direct attention to subsection 5 of section 6 which reads as follows:
For the purposes of this section, forces shall be deemed to be serving together or acting in combination if and only if they are declared to be so serving or so acting by order of the Minister of National Defence, and the relative rank of members of the home forces and of other forces shall be such as may be prescribed by regulations made by His Majesty.
Just what is meant by "regulations made by His Majesty"? Does it mean by His Majesty as advised by the British government or as advised by the government of one of the other nations of the British commonwealth in the case of Canada, our own government? Also is there not a possibility that section 6 will be construed as giving to the Minister of National Defence power which up to the present time we have assumed would be exercised only by parliament itself? I raise that question more particularly because of



Visiting Commonwealth Forces
the wording of section 8, which we have not yet reached. When we come to section 8, it will be noticed that as regards any naval force it says:
So far as regards any naval force and the members of any such force, the provisions of this act shall be deemed to be in addition to and not in derogation of such of the provisions of any act of the parliament of the United Kingdom or of the parliament of any other part of the commonwealth as are for the time being applicable to that force and the members thereof.
While that section is there with reference to the naval forces, there is no similar section with respect to the army or air forces, and the omission of a similar section with regard to the army and air forces seems to me to lend added significance to the powers that are given to the Minister of National Defence under subsection 5.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is a very simple
explanation for that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I saw the
explanation, but I did not regard it as very satisfactory. However we shall come to that section later on.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I believe if the right hon.
leader of the opposition will look at the definition of the term "member" where it is used in this bill he will notice that it applies to an individual person, either an officer or one serving in the ranks.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
"Member" does not apply
to any particular ship of the naval service, or any particular company, regiment or battalion of the home forces or of visiting forces. The definition shows that the term "member" applies to an individual person and not to a company.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I saw that, but I think the minister will admit that if the Minister of National Defence wished to do so he could name a sufficient number of members to include a squadron, regiment or any other body.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
He would have to name
dozens of them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: You would have broken formation, in that event.

The house seems to be passing this bill largely out of respect for the opinion of the Prime Minister that it is necessary and appropriate so to do, because there is no doubt that the language of the bill is so horribly involved, and such long sentences are

used that it is very difficult for the ordinary individual to have any accurate understanding of it. May I ask the Prime Minister if it was agreed at the Imperial economic conference or elsewhere, among the British commonwealth of nations, that this act should, so to speak, be a standard act that would be passed in these terms by British nations', or is this legislation merely indigenous to Canada? Is there any record of other nations in the commonwealth having passed such legislation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. member who has just spoken would turn to page 2 of the bill he would find an extract from the summary of proceedings of the Imperial economic conference of 1030. It will be observed that the report was very simple but-
It was impossible to more than examine some aspects of the practical problems which will be involved in the carrying out of the recommendations contained in paragraph 44 of the report of the conference on the operation of dominion legislation.
It is assumed that all governments will desire to take such action as may be necessary to secure (1) that the military discipline of any of the armed forces of the commonwealth when present, by consent, within territory of another, rests upon a statutory basis. . . .
The reason for that is that the Army Act no longer applies to this part of the British Empire, it being passed at Westminster and1-
12) that there shall be no period of time during which the legal basis of military discipline could on any ground be impeached.
That is for purposes of discipline and control.
The methods by which the above two objects can best be attained must necessarily be a matter for the government themselves.
As the action to be taken to give effect to the recommendations contained in paragraph 44 of the report of the conference on the operation of dominion legislation is likely to take some time, it was agreed that all the governments concerned will take such steps as may be necessary to provide against possible difficulties d-uring that period.
In 1929, it will be remembered, a commits tee met in London to draft legislation to give effect to the principles enunciated in the 1926 conference. The then Minister of Justice represented the Dominion of Canada. Their recommendation did not undertake to draft this bill, but in 1930, when the matter was referred to the appropriate committee, resolutions were arrived at which are set out on page 2 of the notes to the bill. And this bill represents not the draftsmanship of the Dominion of Canada but a bill which is assumed to represent the views of all parts of the commonwealth, subject to changes in terminology and matters of that kind which

Visiting Commonwealth Forces
may be made necessary because of local conditions. I believe the right hon. gentleman said he had the British bill before him this afternoon.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, I was
referring to the convention concerning exhibitions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I understand; that was
in connection with another matter. When the hon. member for Comox-Alberni asks whether or not action has been taken by any other countries, I must answer that I am not definite as to the number who have passed this legislation. My understanding is that it has been passed, but of course in England they still pass their Army Act. The only difference is that the Army Act does not now extend beyond the confines of the United Kingdom, and, of course, the colonies included in matters of that kind. It does not extend to the Dominion of Canada; therefore we are passing this bill.
With regard to the point made by the right hon. leader of the opposition, I do believe that the note appended to section 8 is adequate explanation of the situation. That is, when the matter came before the council of external affairs we settled the general terms of the bill. Section 8 makes it clear that inasmuch as the Army and Air Force Acts are dependent for their force and effect upon the Army and Air Force Annual Act paissed annually by the parliament of the United Kingdom and are no longer, in themselves, subsequent to the passing of the statute of Westminster, applicable to Canada, we felt that we should take some steps in statutory form by appropriate legislation to deal with the position. We already had dealt with the military side of it in our Militia Act; we have already dealt with the air side of it in our Air Force Act, and we have dealt with it in a limited way under our Naval Act. Inasmuch as it has to be prefectly clear that there shall be no confusion of authority section 8 states:
So fair as regards any naval force and the members of any such force, the provisions of this act shall be deemed to be in addition to and not in derogation of such of the provisions of any act of the parliament of the United Kingdom or of the parliament of any other part of the commonwealth as are for the time being applicable to that force and the members thereof.
Because there may be-and I believe it is contended there are-some provisions in United' Kingdom legislation that are still of empire scope with respect to naval matters. That is the position, as I understand it.
I shall not ask to have the bill taken out of committee until I can ascertain definitely whether or not all of the countries affected have passed legislation, and whether or not my information in this connection is exactly correct, because I wish to make perfectly clear the position of Canada with respect to this legislation. In 1926 we made it abundantly clear that we would be responsible for legislation of this character; in 1929 a committee met for the purpose of determining what statutory enactments would be necessary to give effect to the principle. In 1930 the legislation was agreed upon, in form, there being two or three sections left open until after, in this country, we had a conference of the premiers of the provinces in order that they might agree to certain sections of the statute of Westminster. Inasmuch as there would then be, after the passing of the statute and the expiration of the Army Act of that year, no authority dealing with this matter, it becomes essential that we should pass the necessary legislation. I do not know whether or not properly speaking it should not have been passed last year, but in conference with the officials of the department it was made clear that in keeping with our obligations and our position with respect to visiting forces which might, with our consent come to this country, or with respect to the union of forces from another part of the commonwealth with our own, there should be uniformity, and that the legislation should be enacted. That is the reason for it being before the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am pleased to know the Prime Minister says that he will allow the bill to remain in committee. In that connection may I point out to him that I believe his remarks left the impression with hon. members-certainly they did with me-that he is of the opinion that before any of the forces of Canada, whether they be militia, air or naval, can be placed at the disposition of another part of the empire or on service abroad, parliament must be summoned in the first instance and give its consent. The right hon. gentleman nods his head in approval. I believe he will find that such is not the case. I remember that at the time of the Chanak incident in the near east in 1922, we were asked if we would place at the disposition of His Majesty certain Canadian forces. The reply given at that time was that we believed public opinion in Canada would demand, in the first instance, the summoning of parliament, and the authorization by parliament of any forces to be sent abroad

Visiting Commonwealth Forces
I do not think there is any statute which places that obligation upon parliament. I believe under the Militia Act and also under the Naval Act the governor in council has power in time of emergency to place the forces of Canada at the disposal of His Majesty in different parts of the world. But if parliament is not in session at the time, it will have to be summoned within so many days.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Is that for overseas service?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If it is regarded as an emergency, which may affect this dominion it may be in any way. That is the law as it stands. I submit that under the wording of this act, in the light of that icircumstance, the governor in council could rtake the military, naval or air forces and place them at the disposal of His Majesty in parts of the British Empire or in other parts of the world, at the instance of the governor in council himself, and not at the instance of parliament. I think it most important that it should be understood that the forces of this country are not to be placed, at all events, by virtue of anything in this act, at the disposal of His Majesty without parliament being summoned and so authorizing in the first instance, or in other words that it should be made quite clear that this act is intended primarily to further efficiency and cooperation through training in times of peace.
How could they do that unless parliament was summoned to vote the money?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
They could do it as they have done a multitude of things; the government could go ahead and meet the necessary expenses by issuing governor general's warrants, or on its own credit and ask parliament to ratify its action later on. I should like to read to my hon. friend the section of the Militia Act, which is chapter 132 of the revised statutes of 1927. Section 64 reads:
The governor in council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
Then section 66 states:
Whenever the governor in council^ places the militia, or any part thereof, on active service, if parliament is then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall be issued for the meeting of parliament within fifteen days, and parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation, and
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]
shall continue to sit and act in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
Sections 19 and 21 of chapter 139 of the revised statutes of 1927 respecting the naval service of Canada are similar, and I submit that under the provisions of these statutes it would be entirely possible for the governor in council to place the different forces of Canada at the disposition of His Majesty in other parts of the world without having parliament in session and without the authority of parliament for so doing. In addition I submit that it would be within the power of the Minister of National Defence himself under the provisions of the bill now before us to transfer those forces to a single command, all this before parliament had any say in the matter at all. I believe that phase of the matter should be looked into very carefully before we proceed finally with the bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was about to read sections 64 and 66 of the Militia Act, but I think the right hon. gentleman will observe two things. First, there is a limitation placed upon the power of the governor in council. If forces are sent beyond Canada it must be for the defence of Canada.
It always has been so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the first point. Then it is provided that parliament must be called to meet within fifteen days in any event. That being so I submit that my original statement that there could be no dispatch of troops from this country without the consent of parliament is strictly true, for it would be impossible to mobilize and send any body of troops from this country in fifteen days. That at least has been the constitutional position that always has been taken in this country, that even for the defenoe of Canada there can be no such thing in practice as troops leaving the country without parliament having given its consent. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has raised the point upon which I think the argument always has been founded, that since parliament must meet within fifteen days and since there can be no warrants issued after parliament meets in order to vote the money, it therefore follows that parliament must give its pronouncement yea or nay upon the matter by providing or refusing to provide the necessary money.
I believe this meets the difficulty raised by the right hon. gentleman. There has been no change in these statutes for a matter of thirty-five or forty years. We always have predicated the movement of armed forces out of

Visiting Commonwealth Forces
Canada upon the assumption that it was necessary for the defence of Canada. Then, the governor in council having taken the requisite action as an executive act, since the obligation is to call parliament within fifteen days before any expenditure is made and before the troops in fact are dispatched, it follows in the very nature of things that if parliament met and declined to vote the money an expedition would be abortive and could not function. That is the law as I understand it; I believe that has always been the law in this country since we have had to consider these questions. Let me repeat that no troops can leave this country to engage in military operations without the consent of this parliament. I believe that is a correct statement of the position in view of sections 64 and 66 of the Militia Act.
Now let us turn to the Naval Service Act. The real reason for section 80 appearing in the terms in which it does appear will be found in section 46 of the Naval Service Act, which reads:
The Naval Discipline (Dominion Naval Forces) Act, 1911, enacted by the parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland shall apply to the naval forces raised by the Dominion of Canada and the ships provided for such naval forces, subjeot to the modifications, adaptations and exceptions set out in the last preceding section.
The preceding section has to do with the Naval Discipline Act of 1866 and all the amendments thereto, because in 1918 this parliament thought it desirable to adopt in that way the provisions of the statute passed by the United Kingdom in order to secure, as other dominions had secured, a measure of uniformity in the administration of the naval forces. As the right hon. gentleman has remarked, the Air Force Act deals with a new arm of the service, about which all our legislation is more or less experimental.
Is this not a fair way to put it: There has been no change in the substantive law of this country with respect to armed forces, naval or military, for many years. Even the great war did not bring about a change. Our naval act is a relatively new act, which was passed some fourteen or fifteen years ago, and that statute involved a great deal of labour because it had to do with conditions which were entirely different, since the movement of ships at sea is entirely different from the movement of forces on land. I understand that section 80 was passed because of the fact that under the statute we passed, adopting in terms the British statute, there is a residuum of authority resting in the central power. Mark you, it covers not the home forces of Great Britain but the naval forces of the dominions; that is section 46.
That is my understanding of the situation as it now exists. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman has had occasion during his legislative experience to deal with the Dominion Naval Forces Act of 1911, which I think came into force during the first eight months of that year. It was passed at Westminster, I believe following the Imperial conference of that year, as being a statute that embodied an agreement at which all the prime ministers were able to arrive, not to interefere with the autonomy of each of the dominions but to preserve uniformity of administration in connection with the naval forces of the dominions, if it was thought desirable' by the people of the dominion affected to utilize their forces for a common purpose. As this section stands it merely provides that by subsection 4, to which attention has been directed, we shall treat one from abroad within the commonwealth as though he were a Canadian, and the statutes of the other dominions treat a Canadian as though he were a New Zealander or Australian for the purposes of common command if there be such. I do not think it possible to say that any troops could be moved out of this country under any circumstances unless parliament gave its assent; firstly, because fifteen days is a period of time which would certainly elapse before mobilization and movement could be completed; and secondly, no government would move forces out of this country if on calling parliament such action were negatived by nonprovision of the moneys necessary to pay for the expedition. Therefore the first statement I made is I think a statement that has been made in this house frequently and generally accepted as true, that there could be no movement of forces out of Canada for the defence of Canada unless this parliament had approved.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I just make doubly clear the position I take in the matter. I assume that this act has really been drafted by the British government and not by our own government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No; I would not say it has been drafted either by the British government or by our own. I think it is fair to say that it was drafted by a committee of all the dominions. The hon. member who sits behind the leader of the opposition, my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth, was himself present in England in 1929 and must know something of the circumstances in connection with the discussion of this particular aspect of the matter. In 1930 when I came in I found it regarded as having been, shall I say, a fact accomplished, the only question

Visiting Commonwealth Forces
being as to how to give expression to the common purpose, and the legislation now before the house is legislation which has been agreed upon by the parties, subject to such variations as local conditions bring about.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Whoever drafted it undoubtedly had in mind two things, first of all the providing of means whereby the forces of the empire might operate together in times of peace with a view to preparing for more efficient service in time of war. That I think is the first object of the measure -that . in the event of this parliament deciding in time of war to place its forces at the disposition of the empire as a whole there would be practices which would be known, and methods adopted, which would facilitate, expedite and ensure effective cooperation. Some measure of the kind here proposed is necessary in order to enable this preparation in time of peace to take place. There is another object which I think would also be in the minds of those who had the drafting of the measure, and that is the possibility of the different forces of the empire serving together in time of war, and that the second object was so to draft the enactment at the moment as would make its provisions applicable also in time of war. Both these objects may be necessary and desirable, but I am inclined to believe that in drafting the measure those who have had the matter in hand have gone a step further than has been heretofore intended by anything this parliament has sanctioned or contemplated, and certainly anything from what he has said the present Prime Minister has in mind, and have made it possible for a subsequent administration say, if they desired so to do, to have certain of the forces of Canada placed under a single command prior to the time of this parliament's meeting. If there could be added to the act a clause which would ensure that in so far as its provisions are concerned they shall in time of war be effective only after parliament itself has given its consent to such a step, I think that would be advisable and would place matters beyond any doubt.

May I say a word following what my leader has said. Section 6 is the section that gives me some difficulty, as perhaps it has also the Prime Minister and my leader. We have persistently and insistently contended that there should be no unity of command without consent; that is the point on which Canada and the other commonwealths have been very strong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think that is secured.

I was going to speak
about that. Wrhen our troops went overseas unity of command was effected by putting all the forces under Field Marshal Haig, but only by consent; and later when all the allied forces were put under Marshal Foch it was the same thing. Subsection 4 of section 6 makes a slight inroad on that, and I should like to have the Prime Minister, while the matter is under deliberation after the committee rises, consider the question whether at least there should not be action by the governor in council rather than the Minister of National Defence. I am the last one to derogate from the responsibilities, the functions and the dignities of that high office, but at the same time this is the disposition of troops by His Majesty's representative, who is commander in chief of the forces, and therefore it seems to me to be an act solemn and serious enough to have the approval or the consideration of His Majesty's privy council. It is all very well to have visiting forces here, each one under its own command.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That always has been so.

Yes, and to invest those
in charge of visiting forces with sufficient authority to carry out commands and enforce discipline. But when you combine forces you do something that has not been done before, and it should not be simply an order of the Minister of National Defence, because immediately you have done that you may have altered completely the ranks of the officers in the forces. The provision is that, automatically, there is unity of command the moment the minister gives his consent to the combination. Unity of command is effected under the officer of senior rank, whoever it may be, and further than that I notice that subsection 5 provides that the relative ranks of members of the home force and of other forces shall be such as may be prescribed by regulations made by His Majesty. It does not say whether His Majesty is to be advised by the government of Canada or by the government of the United Kingdom and I do not know what the Prime Minister has in mind. It would seem to me as if it were intended to be His Majesty in the right of the United Kingdom. I think we should have some say in deciding on the relative seniority of ranks of officers who make up the combined force.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In view of what has been said I shall discuss the section more fully with the legal officer of the Department of External Affairs and the chief of the general staff. It may be possible that the construction placed

Business of the House
upon the section is as wide as the hon. gentleman opposite suggests, but that was not my understanding of it when I came to the house with it. I shall therefore ask to have the section stand until I have had an opportunity of discussing it and reporting to the house exactly what the views of the legal adviser of the department and of the chief of the general staff may be.
Section stands.
On section 7-Application of act to mandated territories, colonies and other territories.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As regards
this section, it sems to me it might as well be dropped out of the Canadian act. What it really does is to authorize the governor in council to place any of the forces of Canada in other parts of the British Empire for the purpose of joining in service with forces in other parts of the empire in respect of mandated territories and in respect of the defence of colonies, or to services in some other force to be rendered to colonies. Unless we are going to take upon ourselves the obligation of agreeing to let our forces be placed generally at the disposal of other parts of the empire, I think that clause might well be dropped. I notice in the explanatory note it says that it is probable the provisions of this section will rarely be evoked and that it will be necessary to make a special order in council on each occasion. I really do not see why the section should be there at all. It is going to place by inference a new obligation on this country with respect to cooperating with other parts of the British Empire in their special defence relations to colonies and mandated territories.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the right hon.
gentleman has an entirely erroneous view as to section 7. What is intended is that in the rare case of the forces of any colony or mandated territory desiring to visit here, with our consent, this shall apply; because there is a limitation to commonwealth forces, namely forces of the British commonwealth of nations, and unless this provision were here it could not be applied to either mandated territories or colonies. The statute is extended by section 7 to meet that situation. When I first saw the statute I am free to say that my view was not very different from that of the right hon. gentleman himself. But it will be observed that-
This act shall, subject to such exceptions, adaptations and modifications as the governor in council may direct, apply

* The note indicates that it is thought the provisions of the section will rarely be evoked; yet it is desirable to make provision
for such a case in the statute. Certainly it does not contemplate a force being placed at the disposal of any central authority for use in mandated territories or colonies; that is clear. Such a power could not be derived by implication, and I think on mature consideration the right hon. gentleman will agree that it is desirable to provide in the one statute at the one time for contingencies that may arise with respect to these other territories that form part of the British Empire, namely the dominions, that constitute the commonwealth, as well as (a) the colonies and (b) the mandated territories under the League of Nations, for which responsibility rests with us as a signatory to the league, as well as others.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: To an interpretation such as the Prime Minister places on this section I would take no exception, and will be quite satisfied if that is the correct interpretation. As I read the section, piecing it together with other sections, it seemed to me that it gave to the governor in council at any time power to deal with the forces of Canada as a whole for service generally in connection with mandated territories and colonies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not my understanding. If it were I should not ask the house to pass it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps section 8 had
better stand with section 6, in view of the observation made by the right hon. gentleman.
Progress reported.

subtopic: DECISION TO DEFER CONSIDERATION OF BILLS ON ORDER PAPER

I would not take exception to what the Prime Minister suggests were it not that I asked specifically at the
New Westminster Elevator

close of Friday evening of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), who was leading the house at the time, as to whether it was understood that the railway measure would not be proceeded with to-day, and I got the direct assurance that it would not. gentleman understands that since Friday many events have transpired that make it desirable at least to reconsider many things from a different angle than heretofore. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
