Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I have a very important matter to bring to the attention of the government and one which I think ought to be discussed. It relates to the New Westminster elevator. I have hesitated to bring this matter before the house in order to see if this undertaking which was commenced in 1928 would operate successfully. But there are certain serious matters concerning it which I think should now be brought to the notice of the government.
The history of the elevator is briefly this. After years of endeavour it was decided to

construct an elevator on the Fraser river. I might say that we in the lower Fraser valley and in the vicinity of New Westminster look upon the Fraser as the greatest river in the whole of Canada, if not on the American continent. After years of endeavour the government of the day was persuaded to assist in the construction of an elevator on the Fraser river in the vicinity of New Westminster. About that time a company was formed called the Fraser River Elevator Company. This company was formed with a view to getting control if possible of this elevator or ownership of it after it was constructed. The company consisted chiefly of one man by the name of Samuel McClay. He conceived the idea of forming a company so as to have control of this elevator. According to the return furnished to me by the provincial government last September the company consisted of this Mr. McClay and a Walter A. Wilson, chartered accountant, both of 207 Hastings street west, Vancouver. It was capitalized at $25,000. I am in some doubt whether any money was actually subscribed outside of the money for legal fees and incorporation expense.
The nominal capital of the company was later increased to $1,000,000, and in these days, when watered stock is under criticism, I would ask the house to take note of the fact-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It might be well to remember that this is a provincial, not a dominion company.

Yes, it is a provincial company. The information given to me from the provincial government at Victoria is to the effect that the company was originally capitalized at $25,000 divided into 250 shares of $100 each. These shares were subsequently subdivided into 25,000 shares of SI each and the capital increased to $1,000,000 divided into shares of $1 each. The present shareholders of the company are John Coughlan, who goes under the name of a shipowner, 160,000 shares; Charles Coughlan, of Connaught drive, 160,000 shares; Samuel McClay, now chairman of the Vancouver harbour commission, 300,000 shares, and two others, Mr. Sugarman and Mr. Maclnnes, 100 shares each. That was the report given to me by Mr. Garrett, registrar of companies, Victoria, in September, 1932, and as the Prime Minister has pointed out, this is a provincial company. This Mr. McClay, who is now chairman of the harbour commission, is the man who is said to have been appointed to that commission to look after the personal interests of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

New Westminster Elevator

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I cannot allow any such
observation as that to pass unchallenged; there is not a word of truth in it.

The hon. member will have
to take my word that Mr. Samuel McClay made this statement to me in 1931, in the Chateau Laurier in this city, and I consider my word is as good as that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I simply state on a question of privilege that there is no truth in the allegation made by the hon. gentleman that Mr. MdClay was appointed to any harbour commission to look after my personal interests. The statement is without any foundation in fact and is absurd.

I am glad to hear that, because Mr. McClay made that statement and he made some others to me just as serious, but this one has some bearing on the case I am endeavouring to present to the government. I can say without fear of contradiction that that statement was given to me in 1931 by Mr. Sam McClay in the city of Ottawa.
After it was decided to go ahead with this elevator and after an estimate of some 8600,000 had been given by Messrs. C. D. Howe and 'Company, who were the engineers and who were asked to submit plans, tenders were called for the construction of the elevator and a contract was let to the Stuart Cameron Company of Vancouver, whose tender of $460,279 was the lowest.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What date?

The contract was let on
February 20, 1928, after approval had been received from the Department of Marine. Actual construction was commenced a few days later, but the unusual freshet that occurred in the Fraser river early in May of that year interrupted the work on the foundation and caused a delay of some two months. Before the work had proceeded very far, it was decided to make a change in the construction of at least part of the elevator. I should here like to make a slight criticism in regard to the fact that the change involved an expenditure of some $90,000. It would be interesting to know just how that sum of $90,000 was arrived at, because no credit at all was given for the woodwork for that portion as specified in the contract of $460,000 and I have grave criticism to offer regarding this $90,000 extra having been paid to this company who were constructing the elevator for this change in the plan.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When was the work completed?

It was completed some time in 1929. The engineer's final certificate was issued in April of that year. Other changes made in the original contract to the Stuart Cameron Company were certain additional equipment required by the proposed lessee, changing the piling in dock and revetment from fir to cedar, besides sundry other extras. The contract price of February 20, 1928, was $460,279. An agreement of May 11, 1928, provided for a change from wood to concrete at an additional $90,000, and as I say, no credit whatever was given for that change over and I maintain the $90,000 was an overcharge. There was additional equipment amounting to $11,467.91, and sundry extras, including changing piling in dock from fir to cedar, amounting to $4,635.25.
Owing to the delay occasioned by the freshet and also by a carpenters' strike in the fall of 1928, construction was not completed until April, 1929, when the engineer's final certificate was issued.
In May, 1929, some subsidence in the fill-back of the revetment wall took place, and early in July a portion of the revetment collapsed, while the storage building showed some slight movement towards the river. On the advice of the engineers, work was immediately commenced to strengthen the storage and to repair the damage to the revetment, this work being completed in the fall of 1929 at an extra cost of some $23,000.
Messrs. C. D. Howe and Company, the engineers who had charge of the matter, then reported that the elevator was perfectly safe and could be filled up with grain, but the proposed lessees, who were known as the Fraser River Elevator Company, but who were in reality Mr. Sam McClay and Mr. Coughlan of the city of Vancouver, raised some objection and said that the elevator was unsafe and that they could not take over the lease. They said that they were afraid to put grain into the elevator, although the engineers, Messrs. C. D. Howe and Company, had given a certificate to the effect that the elevator was quite safe and would stand any strain or load in the way of grain. Messrs. McClay and Coughlan from then on raised great objections to taking over this elevator; they placed all kinds of difficulties in the way, stating that they were prepared to take a lease of it, but that they certainly could not do so as in their opinion it was unsafe. They prevailed upon the government to have three engineers appointed to look into the matter,
New Westminster Elevator

and the latter suggested further improvements which were carried out at a cost of $40,000. Plans, specifications and estimates of cost of this work were prepared and were forwarded to the Department of Marine on November 12, 1930, the estimated cost being $40,345.08, including engineering fees. The commissioners had to wait some little time for authority to proceed with the work, pending arrangements being made in connection with finances.
As I have already stated, when the elevator was finished, the company started to find fault with the structure declaring it to be unsafe and accordingly they refused to sign the lease. I believe that the object of the so-called company, consisting of two men, was to obtain at a reduced figure control or ownership of this elevator, which had cost this country in the neighbourhood of one million dollars, including of course all the improvement work done around it. At the outset they had agreed that when the elevator was constructed they would lease it for a period of twenty years at an estimated cost of $700,000. The $700,000 was to include elevator, trackage, wharf, and all pertaining to the elevator. It would have been quite a fine scheme for the company if they had obtained such a lease-and remember they had not put up a cent. Here was the country going to build an elevator and at the end of twenty years the company was going to be the complete owner of it. It would be very nice if any one of us could go to the government and ask them to build a house for us at the country's expense, and we rent it for twenty years and then become the absolute owner. That is just on a par with the scheme of this shadow company for obtaining this elevator. I believe, and I say this in all sincerity, that the object of that company was to so damn the structure that they would obtain possession of the elevator at their own figure, and both Mr. McClay and Mr. Coughlan told me when I met them at the elevator last year that they expected to obtain possession of the elevator over a lease of twenty years for some $500,000. They were going to get it at a reduced figure because they claimed they were entitled to compensation on account of delay in the completion of the elevator, which they claim resulted in a business loss to them and which they maintained the government should pay for. I cannot say definitely at the moment just what amount they claimed from the government or the harbour board as a business loss by reason of the elevator not being completed at the stipulated date. But I know it was some thousands of dollars.
An agreement was then drawn up with the harbour board by which the company was
r.Mr. Reid.]
given possession of the elevator to run it as a kind of storage elevator. They paid nothing for it. The taxes and the expenses of the elevator were borne by the harbour board, which had received loans from the government. This so-called company, The Fraser River Elevator Company, put up no money, but they obtained possession of the elevator. In the agreement which was drawn up it was stated that the company, on request of the harbour board, would move out on notice and give them quiet possession of the elevator. Notice was sent to the company by the harbour hoard quite a number of times to move out, but the company paid no attention to the notice; they simply sat there. I think it should be noted that this company, after they had obtained possession of the elevator, defied legal authority to oust them from it. It is true that the company were making some so-called claim from the government for not being able to obtain possession of the elevator at the time stipulated, in consequence of which they stated they had suffered a business loss which they themselves estimated at some thousands of dollars. But they should never have been given the right of entry into the elevator without putting up some money. There has been nothing but grief since they got in there.
The company I believe made a little money from the operations of the elevator. At various times considerable quantities of corn were brought into the elevator, which the company was operating without paying anything at all to the harbour board by way of lease.
Coming to 1932, the company was notified by the harbour board on several occasions to vacate the elevator. This it refused to do. It paid no attention to the request at all. After the harbour board had brought all the pressure it could to bear upon the company, the board decided to call for tenders for the lease of the elevator to be run as an elevator for grain. Two or three firms tendered, in particular the Fraser River Elevator Company, and the Searle Grain Company. The latter company has some 364 elevators, I believe, in this country and is in the grain business in a large way. Although it was stated by one of our local papers that I seemed to be more in favour of leasing the elevator to Yankee interests than Canadian, I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that the harbour board itself recommended that the lease be given to the Searle Grain Company, a very reliable grain company, which, as I said, operates some 364 elevators in this country. But the tender of the Searle Grain Company was turned down by the Department of Marine and the harbour

New Westminster Elevator
board were notified to give the lease to the Fraser River Elevator Company.
To go back for a moment to the steps that were taken in 1932 to make this so-called company vacate the elevator before lease tenders were called for, the harbour board was pressing this so-called company fairly hard but the Department of Marine sent word by telegram not to press the company any further, and not to put them out, as all the matters in connection with the leasing of the elevator had not been finally settled. I make this criticism regarding the attitude of the Department of Marine, that they did not allow the harbour board forcibly to eject the company from possession of the elevator, of which it had been in possession since 1929 and without any cost to them. The company had been operating the elevator at a profit to themselves since taking it over.
Coming again to the leasing of the elevator, tenders were called for in 1932, and tenders were received from the Fraser River Elevator Company and the Searle Grain Company. The Fraser River Elevator Company offered $20,000, plus one-quarter of a cent a bushel up to six million bushels. If six million bushels had been put through the elevator in a year, that would have amounted to $35,000 a year. The Searle Grain Company offered $33,000 a year cash payable half-yearly.
The harbour board recommended to the Department of Marine that the lease be given to the Searle Grain Company for $33,000 cash, but the department wired the harbour board to give the lease to the Fraser River Elevator Company. I understand that that wire was sent by the hon. Minister of Marine, although the information was given to me that Mr. Ramsay, the head of the grain board, also recommended that the Searle Grain Company were the legitimate ones to get the elevator because they were a reliable company and really in the grain business, and not simply ostensibly in it like the Fraser River Elevator Company, which while operating a grain business was not really in the business, and had no grain connections. It is an actual fact that the New Westminster harbour commissioners had recommended to the government that the lease be given to the Searle Grain Company.
But that is not all; and it would not have been too bad. But the agreement drawn up by the harbour commissioners with the Fraser River Elevator Company provided that the lease was to run for some three years, and that the company was to put up $10,000 cash and $10,000 in bonds, and pay one-quarter of
a cent a bushel up to six million bushels. The company were very eager to get complete charge of the elevator. But up to the present time the information that I have both from the harbour board and others connected with the matter is that this company has not yet put up one cent, although the lease was granted in October last, and although the company has put over one million bushels of grain through the elevator.
Mr. Speaker, I believe urgent steps should be taken in connection with this matter regaining an elevator which has cost the people of Canada nearly a million dollars. It would seem that ever since completion it has been practically controlled and owned by the Fraser River Elevator Company, without them contributing five oents towards it. After a lease being signed in October of last year, despite the fact that about a million bushels of wheat have been run through the elevator, no money is yet forthcoming. My contention is that the government should take steps to see that this firm remain no longer in control, even though they have to be forced out in whatever manner the government deem desirable. In any event the firm I have mentioned should not be allowed to continue operation of the elevator. They have promised to put up money, and the lease calls for it. Having taken possession I do not know whether or not the government will be able to put them out. I know the harbour board would have liked to put them out last year, but were told not to molest them. They are sick and tired of this company.
I bring to the attention of the government the seriousness of allowing a firm such as I have described to have charge of an elevator costing close to a million dollars, and in allowing them possession of that elevator. In my view they should not have been allowed possession. Further, ,the chairman of the Vancouver harbour board should not be allowed to have anything to do with the operation of an elevator on the Fraser river. I make that complaint in all seriousness. No one connected with the harbour board of another port should have private interests in a grain elevator owned by this country.
I make a serious complaint against the company, and ask the government to investigate and to take immediate steps to dispossess the company of an elevator which, as I have stated before, belongs to the people of Canada. The company has put up no money-and I doubt if it has any-not one cent has been contributed by way of rental, even though it made money when it used the elevator for storage purposes, and are now making money.
New Westminster Elevator

I have merely touched, the high spots of all the circumstances. I have information upon which I could easily lay my hands concerning the whole transaction about which I have not spoken. I have not gone into minute details although the circumstances might warrant further discussion. However I believe it would be well if a commission or a commissioner were appointed to look into the whole matter. The government should also investigate the fees paid to engineers. Mr. Howe was engaged as engineer to draw plans and look after the construction of the elevator, and yet we find that over $30,000 was paid to another engineer. In addition to that large sums have been paid to Mr. Howe for his work. I am informed that the $30,000 in engineering fees went to a man named Major Swan. In my view .the whole cost of the elevator should be placed under scrutiny. My main complaint however at the present time principally concerns the firm now in possession, the people who are running the elevator and making profit, but who are not actually in the grain business. Mr. McClay is the one chiefly interested in the business, but he is also chairman of the harbour board of Vancouver, and Mr. Coughlan is one of the chief directors. Two other gentlemen have nominal holdings of one hundred shares each, valued at one dollar a share. This is on the information supplied me from Victoria as to who actually comprise that company. In my opinion the company should be put out of operation, because they are not really interested in the grain business. Either the harbour commission, the government or some responsible grain company should take over the elevator and run it so that the dominion and the country would receive some return for its outlay in the building of the elevator.
I have made my statement in all seriousness, with the desire of having this, the first elevator on the Fraser river, put into successful operation, as I expect to see many more on the Fraser river. It will not operate successfully as long as it is handled by the Fraser River Elevator Company. They have given it a black eye and have brought condemnation on it in every shape and form with a view, as I have said, eventually to obtaining ownership of it at some $200,000 less than its original cost, and without having to put up one dollar.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member (Mr. Reid) has given to the house a most interesting story, but I fear the manner in which he has spoken has left in the minds of
[Mr. Reid.l
hon. members an entirely erroneous impression. The view the hon. member has sought to leave with the house is that the government had entered into a lease of certain government property, namely an elevator, in a most improvident manner, with a company which really had no responsibility. From certain interruptions which I made it will be clear to the house that the origin of the alleged difficulty was before the present government took office.
The facts are comparatively simple. Prior to 1928 very strong pressure was brought to bear upon the then government to construct an elevator on the Fraser river at New Westminster. Those representations culminated in a contract for the construction of such an elevator. Before actual construction was undertaken I understand negotiations were carried on between the company which proposed to construct the elevator and a department of the government. Of that, however, I have no personal knowledge, and therefore cannot give any accurate information. In any case the negotiations culminated in a lease being granted to the company by the preceding government.
A word now, in regard to the construction of the elevator. I believe the superstructure, as a whole, was well done. But a question was raised by Mr. McClay in 1928, who was a member of the lessee company, concerning the adequacy of the foundations. I believe he is on record as complaining that the provision made by the engineers at the time of construction in 1928 was not sufficient, because in his opinion the erosion caused by the flow of the Fraser river would probably result in the loaded elevator slipping. This is what actually occurred: When the elevator was finally constructed and possession was taken by the lessees, the insurance companies refused to place any insurance upon grain stored in the elevator. The result was that the lessees could not use the elevator. The point raised by the engineers of the insurance company was that if a load were put into the elevator it would probably slide into the river, resulting in a complete loss. As I have said, the lessees could get no insurance upon grain placed in the elevator; consequently, while in the first year they did pay certain rentals, they were deprived of the opportunity of doing business, and their guarantees and banking arrangements were to them only a dead loss.
When the present government took office we took action. We appointed a committee of engineers to examine the point raised regarding foundations, and my recollection is that that committee, composed of reputable

New Westminster Elevator
and experienced engineers of the government, reported that certain work costing approximately $300,000 would have to be done in order to make the structure suitable! for occupation as an elevator. Of course it must be borne in mind by all hon. members that an elevator must carry a tremendous weight when it is loaded with grain. I think this elevator has a capacity of something like one million bushels, though of that I am not sure. In any case, the weight would be terrific, and this committee of engineers decided that work to cost about $300,000 would have to be done before the elevator was safe for occupancy. So steps were taken-I confess frankly very reluctantly by the government of the day-to spend this $300,000; it was felt that here was a structure costing half a million dollars or more which was useless unless this subsequent work was done. So this government authorized the harbour commissioners to have the work done, the government advancing the money, and the work was done and the elevator declared suitable for occupancy as a grain elevator.
Then there was a dispute between the lessees and the new government as to what damage they were entitled to, if any, and as to what amended terms should be offered for the occupancy of the elevator. That dispute continued for some time. The Fraser River Elevator Company made certain claims for damages; they claimed that allowances should be made for losses for lack of occupancy and for money expended during the period of dispute. Then, if I remember correctly, the harbour commissioners of New Westminster were waited1 upon by another company, called the Searle Grain Company, who made offers for the elevator. This, of course, was subsequent to the elevator being repaired and made suitable for occupancy. The lessees, the Fraser River company, who had possession in name only and who had been unable to do business because of the difficulty with regard to construction, naturally protested the loss of the property and the handing it over to another company. There was a hiatus, a period of time when there was more or less a dispute. The final settlement with the Fraser River Company-I am speaking now with a little hesitancy as I have not the documents before me, but I think I am correct- was that the company agreed to waive their claim for damages provided they were given free and safe occupancy of the building, and to pay a rental of $20,000 a year as indicated by my hon. friend and a quarter of a cent per bushel for the grain which passed through the elevator. I believe they represented that
they expected to move from four million to six million bushels yearly through the elevator. The other company offered $35,000, my hon. friend says.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
My recollection is that
they offered $22,500 and subsequently increased the offer, but I do not think it went to $35,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am not in a position
definitely to dispute that figure, but I know their original offer was nothing like that. True, the matter was discussed by the Department of Marine, as all these matters are, with the harbour commissioners, and that was done in this case particularly in view of the fact that in the meantime we had advanced the necessary money to correct the defects in construction. True, the Department of Marine was in touch with the situation there, necessarily and properly so. Finally, however, having in mind the several years during which the Fraser River company had not been given quiet possession and had been unable to get insurance or do business, it was decided that they were entitled to some consideration, and that consideration was given them. Briefly these are the facts and that is the story.
Now I wish to refer to several observations made by the hon. member in presenting his case. He complains very bitterly that a change was made during the period of construction and that an additional $90,000 was spent. If that is so it was spent by my hon. friends apposite; I am not complaining, but my hon. friend complains. He spoke of it several times, and seemed to insinuate that possibly there was something in the nature of a scandal behind it. I know nothing of it and have never heard of it. My hon. friend may know something that I do not know, but that was what I gathered he intimated. If so he should inquire from hon. gentlemen opposite who had control of the whole situation at that time. I want to make it abundantly clear that I am making no such insinuation myself.
In the second place the hon. gentleman calls into question Mr. Howe, the engineer. All I have to say is that Mr. Howe was retained by my predecessor in the Department of Trade and Commerce for the expert engineering on all the government elevators constructed during the period they were in office.

I said Mr. Howe was the
engineer in charge and that he O.K.'d the plans. I made no criticism of Mr. Howe.
27d6
New Westminster Elevator

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Very good. It is rather
a narrow difference when you criticize a given plan or operation O.K.'d by an individual and at the same time exculpate that individual from all blame. My hon. friend can do that if he likes; it takes a more adroit mind than mine. I have this to say, however:	Mr. Howe is no particular personal friend of mine but he has been recognized by the United Grain Growers, by the pools, by the preceding government, by my predecessor in office and by almost everyone in Canada who has had anything to do with elevator construction as one of the most experienced elevator engineers in Canada. That is not my testimony; it is the testimony of all those to whom I have referred, so I think in retaining Mr. Howe the preceding government did a perfectly proper thing. I am not calling him in question at all, but my hon. friend is doing so. Mr. Howe was responsible for the plans of that elevator. He designed them and he supervised construction.
He however washed his hands of the elevator later on when they interfered with him.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: When who interfered with him?
When the harbour board interfered. Here is his letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The fact is that Mr. Howe was in charge. I do not call him in question nor do I call in question the Department of Marine prior to 1930, when this elevator was built. I do say this was a very difficult piece of ground upon which to construct an elevator, and an engineering error may have been made. The fact is that no insurance company would insure the building; certain work had to be done to put it into proper shape, and this work was done. No blame in this regard lies at the door of this government, nor am I placing the blame on any other government. I am merely stating facts. My hon. friend goes on to say that Mr. Howe was paid a huge fee; those are his words, and the suggestion is that he did not earn it. I suggest that Mr. Howe is an honourable man in his profession, and is entitled to his fee.

It was the other engineer to
whom I referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am just coming to that, and I am sorry my predecessor in office, the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) is not in his seat. Major Swan is well known to the friends of my hon. friend, the members of the former government; he is a gentleman

who frequently was retained by the government in these matters. As a matter of fact, if I am not mistaken, at the very time he was engaged on this work he was consulting engineer for the Vancouver harbour commisr sioners. I knew Mr. Swan before he went overseas and I have known him since his return. I know him as an honourable man, a gentleman of repute, an engineer of parts and a very strong supporter of hon. gentlemen opposite. My hon. friend says he was paid $30,000. If he received that fee I have no doubt that it was in accordance with the standards of engineers, but there again that has nothing to do with it. That was under the control of the government who preceded us. I am not calling it in question and I think my hon. friend had better discuss that with the gentleman with whom he is now associated.
My hon. friend says that the contract was let in February, 1928. He says that the elevator was completed in April, 1929, and that there was a refusal on the part of the Fraser River Elevator Company to take the lease. So there was. There was a refusal after they had taken possession and found that they could not get insurance. They could do no business in the elevator and it was perfectly proper that they should refuse under these circumstances. Then my hon. friend brings in at very considerable length the organization of the Fraser River Elevator Company and he repeatedly, time after time, stressed the fact that Mr. Sam McClay, president of the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners at the present time, was a member of that company. That company was organized-I am speaking from memory-some time in 1926 or 1927. At that time Mr. McClay was in private life and was quite entitled to engage in any line of business he wished. He had nothing to do with the then government and nothing to do with this government so far as that period of time was concerned. He was a member of that elevator company, I believe. Mr. John Coughlan, a splendid citizen, a man of about seventy-seven years of age, who has carried on business in British Columbia to my own knowledge for thirty years, is a man of repute, a man of substance, and in every sense is entitled to consideration in any business deal to which he places his hand or gives his attention. After Mr. McClay became chairman of the harbour board in Vancouver he was dissociated from this company and had nothing to do with it.

He still possessed 300,000
shares.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is probably the
original record.
That was last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext: There is no record of a year's rental. They put up $30,000 in bonds which they lifted later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I know that they put up $30,000 in any case, but they had no quiet possession, they were unable to operate, and they could not get insurance. It was in view of these facts that subsequently, when it came to the 1932 period, consideration was given them. I may say to my hon. friend that if that company under its present lease, which is a legal document-and I have no doubt that Mr. Coughlan is held responsible for that; if he is not he should have been-if the company, I say, are violating the terms of that lease, if they are falling down in their part of the agreement, then I have no hesitation in saying that the harbour commissioners certainly should enforce the lease. That is my position and it is as clear as day. They must observe the terms of the lease. I do say, however, that in my opinion the harbour board and the Marine department were not only within their rights but did the fair thing when they permitted the continuance of that lease in the light of the experience which the company had had prior to the rectification of the faulty construction.
My hon. friend in his concluding remarks said that Mr. McClay, who is president of the Vancouver Board of Harbour Commissioners, ought not to have anything to do with the company. With that I entirely agree, and my information is that he has nothing to do with it. I trust that assurance will calm the perturbation of mind of my hon. friend-

He still takes a supervised
interest in it-his son is running it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My information is entirely to the contrary.

I have, however, seen him
there; I saw him before I came to Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is all I wish to say at the moment, Mr. Speaker. I have not before me the documents and details but the house may, if it wishes to do so, examine the records which will bear out the outline of the situation as I have given it.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Perley (Qu'Appelle) in the chair.

speechtext: No, it is comparatively immaterial.

Perhaps the minister can give some explanation of the activities of this branch.
Supply-Health-Narcotics

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This appropriation is for providing laboratory and1 inspection service dealing with adulteration and misbranding of human food and of drugs employed for the treatment or prevention of disease in mam or animals; the control of export, import and sale of all! habit forming drugs; investigations and prosecutions in connection with traffic in narcotics, and payment of lawyers' fees in connection with 'the various prosecutions; and the protection of the public by .seeing that all proprietary or patent medicines sold are of some value and not dangerous, and that false or exaggerated Claims are not made either on the label or in the advertising.
Does the minister carry out the provisions of the act by the aid of the mounted police, or has he special officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The department keeps in close association with the mounted police in reference to the detection and prosecution of cases arising under the narcotics act.

Those are the only officers the minister has to enforce the act?
Mr. MacLAREN; As far as narcotics are concerned wie cooperate with the mounted police. Regarding adulteration of food we have inspectors placed at intervals across the country, twenty-seven or twenty-eight of them. When cases arise reports are sent in to the department, and- food that is suspected is examined in our laboratories and the necessary action taken.
Do the mounted police take charge of the prosecution?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In which case?
Where adulterated food is found and report made to the department and the department is convinced that an offence has been committed, is the matter then placed in charge of the mounted police?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
No, our connection with the mounted police is restricted to narcotics. Food comes under our food inspectors, and the action is taken by the chief inspector.
I might say for the information of the house that while there were a number of reports and prosecutions, in the last two years the principal food which has come under the observation of the department and in connection with which prosecutions have been instituted and fines fixed1 is sausages. I say this for public information as well, that there are certain substances which have been added to sausages in the way of preservatives, and I think per-

haps in thie way of colour, and the department is doing what it can to suppress this adulteration. I .mention it because quite a considerable number of cases have come before the department.
Do I understand that the minister or his department is responsible for the administration: of the Meat and Canned Foods Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is under the Department of Agriculture. The matter of foods comes partly under my department, partly under the Department of Agriculture and also in some cases under the provincial authorities. Misbranding and adulteration of canned foods are dealt with by this department, but on the whole canned foods are under the Department of Agriculture.

Let me make my meaning quite clear. Was the minister or his department privy to or cognizant of or in any way responsible for the perpetration of P.C. 206 that we talked about the other day, in connection with the inspection of canned salmon? It was certainly issued under the provisions of the act dealing with meat and canned foods. I am anxious to know who is responsible for that offspring.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The answer is that the department does concern itself to a small extent with canned foods, that is to say as regards labelling. If it is mislabelled, then the department is concerned.
Do the functions of the inspectors of this department extend only to the labelling of the canned foods, or do they go beyond that?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I understand the hon. member asks, is the department limited to misbranding and mislabelling. That is largely what we are confined to. The Department of Agriculture actually deals with canned foods, but should a case of adulteration be brought to its attention then the department analyzes and reports on the condition.
Is it a fact that the department has inspectors to examine foods that are placed on the market?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Well there is a Meat and Canned Foods Act, that is specially under the Department of Agriculture. I was suggesting a moment ago that there are various departments and organizations having to do with the adulteration of food-the Department of

Supply-H ealth-N arcotics
National Health, the Department of Agriculture, which deals particularly with canned foods, and food under the provincial authorities.
At this point will the minister explain how the work is divided? Surely there is not any overlapping. I understand from the minister there are three bodies which deal with the adulteration of food.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I quite agree that there is a possibility of confusion as to just where the responsibility lies in different cases. This is a memorandum on the subject.
The control of the manufacture and sale of foodstuffs comes under the Department of Pensions and National Health, the Department of Agriculture, the provincial departments of health and the municipal departments of health. The Department of National Health prescribes standards of quality and fixes the limitation of variability permissible in any article of food. Through its inspectors and analysts certain foodstuffs are collected, examined and analysed for adulteration and misbranding. Under the Meats and Canned Foods Act the Department of Agriculture controls foodstuffs that are manufactured for export and interprovincial sale, according to the standards of quality set up by the Department of National Health where they apply, hnd, in other instances, according to their own standards. All manufacturers who export and sell interprovineially are obliged to obtain a permit from the Department of Agriculture. The inspectors of this department supervise the foodstuffs during the course of manufacture and examine them after they are placed on the market. In some isolated instances provincial departments of health have set up standards of quality for certain foodstuffs, for example, milk, but in the main they follow the standards set up by the Department of National Health. Municipal departments of health confine their activities to the examination of premises in which foodstuffs are stored or exposed for sale. I think that indicates how the work is apportioned.
Does the department regularly analyze all now patent medicines that' are put on the market before they are allowed to be sold?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
They are not examined
until application is made to the department to have them registered. When the application is duly made, they are passed on by the department.
They are examined?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Yes. Patent medicines
are examined. If they are not in accordance with the labelling, action is taken.

Some time ago I asked a question and I do not think the minister got the purport of it. What I want to know is the activities of this department in enforcing the Opium and Narcotic Drugs Act, how much money was spent under it, what success the department has had, and a resume of what it has done during the past twelve months.

speechtext:
In reference to opium
and narcotics, there were the following expenditures :
Legal services, $32,541.07; witness fees and expenses, $315; secret investigational work, $291.92-Total, $33,147.99.

legal services, will the minister give the names of the lawyers who received this very large sum of money in these times of depression?

Higher courts mean higher
fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
That is the total legal
expense in connection with narcotics.

speechtext:
The expenditures for
legal services were as follows: Elie Beauregard, Montreal, $1,757.10-
He is a good Liberal.

May I say for the benefit of my hon. friend from St. Ann that Mr. Monette is a good Conservative.

speechtext: One must remember that a large percentage of these cases are in the province of Quebec, particularly in Montreal.
Is that persecution or prosecution?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He has acted I think in nearly all the Montreal cases. Incidentally I may say that it is desirable to obtain the services of those who have had experience and training in this peculiar class of case.
I can quite understand the reasoning of the minister that we should have barristers who are trained in this particular class of work. When did Mr. Monette's training with the department begin?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He has been handling this class of case for a number of years: I cannot say just how many. The experience of the department is that it is advantageous to have continued those legal men who are familiar with this particular class of case.

I do not wish to embarrass the minister in any way, but I should like to impress on the house that this is a very serious question. Tens of thousands of people in this country are being demoralized by the use of narcotics; and that is one of the big things which this parliament and the country has to fight. I should like to hear from the minister, if I may, what progress has been made in the last twelve months in suppressing the smuggling of opium, the use of which has demoralized tens of thousands of our people. It is one of the really serious questions before the people of Canada. I am not particularly interested in who got the money for enforcing the act, but I am interested in knowing how well the act was enforced and with what results.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The suppression of the illegal use of narcotics is one that is very closely studied by the departmental officers. There is no evidence of an increase; on the whole I believe there is a diminution in the use of narcotics, if the convictions are a guide, and I believe they are a fairly safe guide. The convictions have been as follows, 1925, 835 convictions; 1926, 743; 1927, 490; 1928, 430; 1929, 567; 1930, 458; 1931, 333. So far as one may judge from the convictions, the use of narcotics is less than it was in previous years.

Perhaps the minister
would give us a little further information regarding those convictions. What becomes of the addict who is convicted? Is he punished by being sent to gaol, or is hospital treatment provided for him?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: So far as the penalties are concerned, there are heavy fines or imprisonment, or both. So far as treatment is concerned, arrangements are made for giving suitable treatment to the individual.
What treatment is provided? Does the department pay for the treatment, or how is it provided?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The department does not pay for the treatment.
Who provides the treatment?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It depends upon the man. A man may pay for his own treatment, for instance, or if he is sent to a public hospital he becomes a public charge.

Does the minister say that
a man convicted of a crime under a narcotic act and sentenced to imprisonment is obliged to pay for the treatment he receives as a prisoner?

Supply-Health-Narcotics

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Arrangements are made for the treatment of individuals who are imprisoned.
At whose expense?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
At the expense of the
public. Arrangements are made with the gaol physician who carries on the treatments.

Does the Department of
Pensions and National Health pay the physicians for those treatments?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
We incur no expense.
But in cases where there is no imprisonment we do everything possible. We advise the people affected to go to hospitals or sanataria to receive treatments, and show an interest in the welfare of each individual.

Who carries on the work
of advising and showing interest in the welfare of individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The medical officers of
the department. Then we have a special staff dealing with narcotics, who do all they can, from a humanitarian standpoint, to assist the people affected.

Does this matter not come
under the control of the provincial legislatures? After a successful prosecution the individual goes to an institution, and such institutions are maintained by the provinces, therefore all expenses fall to the provinces.

I understand there are
no provincial institutions to care for narcotic victims. I understand, further, that for a long time there has been an agitation to have the federal Department of Health take steps to provide such institutions. Is the department giving the matter any serious consideration, and is there any likelihood of the government supplying a fund for this purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The view of the department is that the matter is of a provincial nature, and it has not been considered by the government. Outside of that, however, it is the disposition of the department in every possible way to help in connection with this very important matter. While the care of the sick and of those who indulge in narcotics is a responsibility of the provincial legislatures, yet in many cases our own departmental officers can and do help individuals. In any event they are interested in seeing that the best possible treatment is given.

If the federal department assumes the responsibility for locating narcotic victims, and those who are guilty of infractions of the law, one wonders that it does not take any responsibility whatever in connection with relieving the unfortunate condition in which those individuals find themselves. It seems reasonable that if the government assumes the one responsibility it should assume the other concerning the cure of these people.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: As the matter is within the control of provincial legislatures I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. member. I do not believe one would want both federal and provincial governments attempting to do the same thing. As a matter of fact curative measures come under the provincial and not the federal control. Whether or not the action suggested by the hon. member is advisable is a different matter.

Do I understand from
the minister that provincial legislatures have no responsibility concerning trafficking in narcotics, but that the constitution has placed the matter, so far as that angle of it is concerned, solely under the responsibility of the federal government? Do I understand, further, that the federal department takes no responsibility for cure?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have explained what
the department is doing and believe I have covered the ground sufficiently. I do not say that the provinces have nothing to do with the apprehension of offenders, because the fact is that provincial and local police do t'heir duty in connection with the detection of the improper use of narcotics.

The matter of what should be done with narcotic victims is widely debated not only in this House of Commons but throughout the country. As a matter of fact the ordinary hospital is not the proper place to deal with such people. There are institutions throughout the United States where much better treatment is provided than is given in Canada. For a long time there has been an agitation in Canada for provision for similar institutions. So far no provincial legislature has accepted the responsibility of establishing such institutions, and the federal government adopts a similar attitude. In my view this is a matter to which the department should give very serious consideration, because until in Canada we have some means of properly treating these victims, we will not get very far.

I should like to add one or two remarks to what I was saying when the committee rose for dinner. We were talking about the narcotic drug traffic, and I should like to say that there are a few things in Canada which seem to fall between the two stools, the federal government on the one hand and the provincial government on the other. What is the drug traffic? It simply amounts to this, that a number of unscrupulous individuals enter into this traffic and victimize whomever they may for their own profit. Unfortunately the victims often are prominent persons of high social standing, and frequently are women. I can say that without fear of contradiction. Eventually the criminals who sell the drugs, as well as their victims, are brought to justice. Those who indulge in the traffic for purposes of gain are sent to gaol; but the victims also come before a judge and are fined, and what happens? They can be sent to gaol or to hospital, but unfortunately the hospitals will not take in these people unless they have special guardians. So for the most part they have no other place to go but the common gaol.
Before recess I maintained that somehow or other the federal government should make advances to the provincial governments for the construction of institutions where these people could be looked after. Unfortunately some of the first families of the land-and I apeak with knowledge-number victims of the narcotic trade among their members, and there is practically no place to send those people because the hospitals wash their hands [DOT]of the responsibility of looking after them. That is the position in connection with this matter. When I broached the subject to the minister before dinner I was simply reviving an old question that has been discussed in various quarters for a long time. There is no doubt that there is a crying need for at least one institution in every province for victims of alcohol and drugs, where they may be sent for succour.and care and in the hope of being retrieved. When victims of narcotics are sent to common gaols they suffer the torments of

hell and apparently there is no other place to send them. In Manitoba the province has what we call a psychopathic hospital for the care of incipient and minor cases of insanity, and fortunately this hospital does care for these people. There may be other such institutions in Canada, but I do not know of them.
Surely this is a responsibility of the federal government, because the question is a national one. If the government are sufficiently interested in the matter to bother running down these people and taking them to court, at least they should give them some care and consideration after they have been run down. I am bringing up this matter again so that the minister may give it his attention and in the hope that the federal authorities will consult the provincial authorities and provide places for the care of such cases.
