Supply-Health-Hospitals
Marine hospitals, including burial expenses of destitute deceased mariners and grants to institutions assisting sailors, $187,500.
This fund is made up principally of mariners' fees paid in the various ports. Does the government contribute to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
This item provides for
medical and surgical attendance and such other treatment as may be required for sick and injured mariners belonging to vessels that pay sick mariners' dues in conformity with the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act, chapter 186 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. With certain exceptions, dues at the rate of 2 cents for every ton which a ship measures, registered tonnage, is collected from every vessel arriving at any port in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, and from any place out of Canada or from any port in another province; and the revenue thus obtained is generally speaking approximately equal to the expenditure incurred. The department operates a hospital at Sydney, Nova Scotia, and one at Lunenburg for the exclusive use of sick mariners entitled to the benefits of the act. At other ports provision is made as far as possible for care and treatment at contract rates at the various local hospitals. Where there is no marine or designated hospital the collector of customs, who approves the application for treatment, sends the sick mariner to the port physician and if considered necessary provision is made for his care and treatment in some private residence. Owing to the decrease in shipping activities here has been a decrease in the number of vessels paying these dues and also a decrease in the expenditure.

I know all about the operation of the act. What I want to know is whether the fund is entirely taken up for the purpose indicated by the minister or whether there is a deficit to which the government must contribute.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Last year the receipts
were $184,485.47. The previous year they were $201,767.
What were the expenditures?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
For the year 1930-31
they were $209,085.55, and for 1931-32, $208,845.90. In the year 1930-31 the deficit was $7,237.83, and last year, $24,360.43.
Did the government contribute to the deficit out of the consolidated revenue fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There has been a surplus in previous years and with that we have been meeting the deficit.

How much of the surplus
is now left?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Since confederation there has accumulated a net surplus of $273,538.70.

With such a surplus I do
not see why the expenditure should be reduced this year. This is not money that comes out of the government of Canada; it is money contributed by the vessels the sailors on which are supposed to receive this hospital aid when necessary. I cannot see therefore the necessity of reducing the expenditure when it is so absolutely essential to look after these men. In addition to the amounts collected from vessels coming from foreign ports and from vessels sailing from one province to another in Canada under Canadian register there is also a payment made to look after sick or injured sailors locally-fishermen. The fishermen pay into this fund and are looked after locally. The minister says that where-there is no hospital arrangements are made for the treatment locally of sick or injured sailors. I have in mind a fisherman who was injured in the harbour of Shippegan. The vessel to which he belonged had paid sick mariners' dues, and in the course of his calling a codfish hook ran into his hand. There was no local doctor authorized to look after sailors in Shippegan and this man would have had to drive twenty-one miles to see a doctor. He could not stand the drive; the suffering was too great. The sub collector of customs at that port therefore gave the man an order to be treated by a local doctor, but that local doctor not having an appointment through the department has been refused payment for the treatment of this sailor. I hold that the doctor is entitled to payment. It would be a hardship-I will not qualify it with any stronger word-to force a sailor to drive twenty-one miles with a large fish hook stuck in his hand, and that it what this man would have had to do; he would have had to go to Caraquet. He could not undertake that drive, he was treated by the local doctor, and the doctor gets nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I need hardly point out that in emergencies no regulations hold.

Why then was this doctor
not paid? I have the correspondence, and it says that the collector of customs had no authority to order a local doctor to look after this man; he should have sent him to Caraquet.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
He had not under
ordinary circumstances, but in a case of emergency he had every reason to do so. If the hon. gentleman brings the matter to my atten-
Supply-Health-Hospitals

tion, with the name, I shall have that promptly put right. The rule in ordinary cases is that they go to the regularly appointed man only. But in case of emergency these men must be looked after, and the department will see that they are looked after. I presume the hon. member for Gloucester has in his mind the small boats. I think the men who use these small fishing boats are receiving very fair treatment compared with the general medical attendance. For instance in the last year vessels of less than thirty-four tons produced a revenue of $1,236; and on cases of members of crews of these small boats $10,313.82 was expended.
Mr. MaclINNIS:	Would the minister tell
the committee how much of last year's vote was given in grants to institutions for assist ing sailors?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The total is $2,600. It is divided in amounts of $200 to various sailors' institutes on the Atlantic and the Pacific-Navy League of Canada; Sailors' Institute, North Sydney; Navy League, Sydney; Seamen's Mission Society, Saint John; Catholic Sailors' Clulb, Saint John; Catholic Sailors' Club, Montreal; Catholic Sailors' Club, Hochelaga Branch; Montreal Seamen's Institute; Montreal Sailors' Hospital; Catholic Seamen's Club, Quebec; Quebec Seamen's Institute; Vancouver Sailors' Home; Victoria Sailors' Institute. These different organizations received $200 a year towards their facilities for looking after sailors.

Does this item really
constitute a form of insurance that is afforded sailors, or why does the government of Canada give special consideration to sailors as a class?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes, I would consider it a form of insurance. Two cents a ton is charged on vessels coming to our ports from outside the country or the province, to form a fund to pay for the expenses of sick mariners. Otherwise they might be left uncared for or go ashore without proper means of support. The insurance, if you wish to call it so, is paid by the owners of the vessels.

I notice there is a decrease
of $20,000 in this item. I would like the minister to explain why this very important vote is decreased by that amount. He told us a short time ago that there were certain marine hospitals in different parts of the country. These hospitals are kept up by the appointment of marine doctors by the department. In my own town there is a marine hospital which for a number of years has been of great

benefit to the fishermen and sailors coming into that port. After this government came into power the doctor who had had charge of the hospital, a very capable man, was dismissed without cause and another physician, a Conservative, appointed, without reason and without justification. Then for some reason, within eighteen months that new appointee of the Conservative government was dismissed. I would like to know why this very capable doctor was dismissed and another man put in his place.
There must be something wrong about that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is a question that I would prefer to take up with the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough in the department. I suggest that it is not advisable to discuss a matter of that kind here, because I believe it would give rise to harm, certainly to no good. But I wish to say this, very emphatically and without any doubt, that the officer he refers to was not displaced without cause. I suggest that the hon. member come down to the department and I will show him the files; I would rather not put the matter on Hansard unless he insists upon it. Neither that officer nor any other has been displaced without good and proper cause.

Of course I appreciate the minister's delicacy in not wanting to deal with this matter on the floor of the house. The first physician dismissed was a Liberal. Without telegraphing this gentleman or getting his consent to having .this matter discussed publicly here, I am willing to take the responsibility for asking the minister now, without going to his department, why this very capable doctor who had been the physician in the hospital for a number of years and who had the confidence of the fishermen and sailors, was dismissed in 1930. That is the first point. The second thing I want to say is that after this capable doctor was dismissed upon the present government coming into power, a very capable Conservative doctor was appointed-to that hospital and within twelve months that Tory doctor was dismissed without cause. Surely the minister does not want me to go to the department and discuss with him privately why a good Conservative, a man who always voted for the Conservative government, who went out and worked during every one of -the last ten elections, was dismissed without cause as medical officer in the Lunenburg marine hospital. I think it is time the minister should give the public and me the reason why this good Conservative was dismissed without cause.

Supply-H ealth-H ospitals

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I should say that what the 'hon. member has stated is evidence that the department is administering its affairs without regard to politics. As I said, I am not, if I can help it, going to drag the affairs of these men into public in the house. I do not think it is a proper thing, and I ask the committee to support me in that.

I think we have a right to know why these capable men were dismissed. As to the first doctor, I have no objection to that, because by dismissing him the minister and the government have made of him a good canvasser against the present government in the next election.
Why worry?

In the 1930 election, due to
the fact that this first doctor had an appointment from the previous government, he did not stir from his place on polling day; he did not do anything at all to help return the Liberal party to power. Now, of course, since his dismissal, he is a good Grit and in the next election he will go out and work to elect a Liberal candidate. Since this government came into power, without reference to the Civil Service Commission, without reference to anybody except the patronage committee, they appointed a Conservative doctor to take charge of the hospital, but not satisfied with that, within eighteen months after this very capable doctor had been appointed, they dismissed him.
Perhaps he turned Grit.

The cute old fox from Cape
Breton South is right. That former Tory doctor, because of his dismissal, is going to vote Grit and work Grit in the next election. I am not complaining. What I want to know from the government and the minister himself is why this capable doctor, who was a friend of the party and should not have been dismissed, was let out. It is up to the minister and his officials to give reasons for the dismissal of this doctor and the appointment of another Conservative.
Carried.

No. I am going to demand
that the minister give me a good reason for what was done in this case. First, a gentleman of his own profession, of good standing in the medical profession, was dismissed from his position as marine physician because he happened to be a Liberal. I have no particular objection to that. What I want to know is why, after this Liberal doctor was dismissed
and a Conservative appointed, within eight-teen months the latter capable gentleman, who was a Conservative and a good follower of my hon. friend, was dismissed from his position, and I am going to demand an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I can go this far with
my hon. friend. I would do a great deal to meet his wishes. I may say that the first vacancy was caused by death. As regards the other, an investigation was held, the various aspects of the case were looked into and it was decided that his services should be dispensed with.

I agree with the minister that the first dismissal was caused by death, political death. I think I should know exactly what happened in regard to the dismissals from this hospital. It is true that a year before my hon. friend was appointed Minister of National Health, the gentleman who was in charge of the hospital in that town did die, but I had the honour and pleasure of recommending a new man; in fact I recommended not one but two, because they were in partnership. When this government came into power, those gentlemen were dismissed. As I said a moment ago, during the 1930 election they felt that because they were getting SI ,000 in salary from the government, they could not very well go out and work for the Liberal candidate. Therefore, I was delighted that they were dismissed because in the next election they will be the best workers we have in that part of the country. I believe to the victors belong the spoils, and I have accordingly no objection when my hon. friend, of course on representations made by his party- and I am not complaining of that; I would have done the same thing-appointed a good Conservative. It was the proper thing to do. What I do object to is that within twelve or fifteen months after this Conservative, a respectable, efficient physician, who looked after his work and who had the confidence of the fishermen, sailors and citizens of the town, was appointed, he was dismissed. I am sure every hon. gentleman opposite should sympathize with me in my argument, because I am trying to defend their own party. It may be all very well for the minister to try to get by this with a smile, but he must not forget that in that little town where the hospital is situated, the fact that this good Conservative, a reliable physician, was dismissed from his position, would have some reflection on his standing and character in the community. I, who am a neighbour of this man, resent that my hon. friend, for some reason which I do not know, dismissed this capable physician, who had the confidence of the fishermen and sailors, and
Supply-Health-Hospitals

appointed another man in his place. It is due to the community and to the Conservative party that the minister should explain why this was done.
Carried.
With regard to this dismissal and the new appointment, I want to ask the minister whether the new appointment was made by the Civil Service Commission or by his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
All these appointments
are departmental, none being made by the Civil Service Commission-or rather, I understand that for some years there has been an understanding or agreement between the Civil Service Commission and the department, and the latter makes the appointments.

How long has this
agreement been in force between the department and the Civil Service Commission giving power to the former to make the appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That was brought about by an order in council.
When?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It was some time ago,
in 1923.

I happened to be a
member of the committee which investigated the administration of the civil service last year, and what the minister now says simply bears out the evidence that was submitted to that committee, showing that the Civil Service Commission was not performing the functions for which it was created. In nine hundred and ninety cases out of a thousand, before an appointment is made by the Civil Service Commission, it has to be O.K.'d by the head of the department.
You should know.

I should know because
I was a member of that committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The commission does
not appoint these men.

That is what I am
saying.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is what I say.

This is just another
case that goes to bear out the evidence that the Civil Service Commission is not performing the functions for which it was created. As the minister has told us to-night, an agreement is entered into between the head of the department and the commission whereby the commission waives its right to make the ap-

pointment, and in nine hundred and ninety cases out of a thousand it will be found that the department makes the appointment. We had deputy ministers come before that committee last year and point out to us definitely that time after time an eligible list would be presented to the department and be torn up, that a second list would be presented and be torn up, and then the head of the department would invite or suggest to somebody to make application, and that application would go through. The Civil Service Commission is not allowed to function.

Now you have put your
foot in it.

The hon. member for North
Renfrew said that the hon. member for South Battleford had put his foot in it. It would be better if some people would put their foot in their mouth and keep quiet.
The minister said a moment ago that these appointments were made without reference to the Civil Service Commission. My understanding of the order in council of 1923 was that all appointments to positions over $200 had to be made by the Civil Service Commission and be advertised in the regular way, and that positions under S200 were left to the government to fill. If I had my way the party in power would make all the appointments. I agree with my hon. friend from South Battleford that the Civil Service Commission is now and has been purely a camouflage. I see by the newspapers of the last few days that a gentleman from Prince Edward Island is coming to Ottawa to be made chairman of the Civil Service Commission, and that two other gentlemen are to take the places of the two now serving. I say that the best thing for this government to do, especially in view of the economic conditions today, would be to do away with the Civil Service Commission, and let the ministers of the different departments and members of parliament take full responsibility of all appointments of whatever kind.
Coming back to this particular case, the Minister of Health, on the representations of somebody, dismissed a capable Conservative physician.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. That is not the statement I made. I said that an investigation was duly held, as a result of which it was considered advisable to retire this man.

I accept the minister's explanation. I would not for a moment put my judgment against his, and I am sure my hon. friend

Supply-Health-Hospitals
from Long Lake will agree with that. Nevertheless the fact remains that the gentleman who was appointed physician of the hospital in Lunenburg by my hon. friends opposite after they came into power was a capable man, and I still say that there was no reason why he should have been dismissed.
Go and look at the files which the minister has offered to make available to you.

Go and look at the files yourself if you want to see them. You have nothing else to do; I have. I know the circumstances, which my hon. friend does not. He should not try to be smart about a matter that I know all about and that he knows nothing about. I say to my hon. friend from away out on the great prairies, from the ranches of Alberta, if he wants to go over the Rocky mountains, let him go. I come from down by the sea coast.
It is you who want the information.

Then why don't you hold your tongue and let me get it? Surely, Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend must realize that I am capable of getting any information I want, and he need not worry his brains about it.
As I was saying, the Conservative government, after they came into power in 1930, dismissed a Liberal appointee. I have no objection in the world to that; it was the right thing to do from my standpoint. Then they appointed a Conservative to that position. What I do object to is that this capable, efficient, decent, respectable, God-fearing citizen who goes to church every Sunday and teaches in the Sunday school, and who voted Tory-
He is not a Presbyterian, is he?

Pretty nearly; he may be a
Lutheran. This gentleman for some reason or other was dismissed from his position, and there are certain people in the town who cannot understand why that should have been done. I am sure the minister did not do it himself. I cannot believe for a moment that he did it without knowing something about it.
Mr. MacLAJtEN:	The hon. member cannot put it that way. I have said that an investigation was held.

The minister says that an
investigation was held. Being a political
partisan as I am, and as you are, Mr. Chairman, I cannot understand why the minister had an investigation of a good Tory, for this man was a Conservative partisan, a follower who had given good service to the Conservative party, as well as to the hospital, to the fishermen and the sailors. Why should there be an investigation of a man when there was nothing against his character or his ability in performing his duties?

It is hard for a Liberal to
understand that.

It is only a hard-hearted Tory who would do it. A Liberal would never do it. The fact remains that this good Conservative was dismissed from his position, and another good Conservative was appointed. What I should like to know from my hon. friend is what investigation took place resulting in the dismissal of this good Conservative, and what particular qualifications has the new appointee for the position?
In other words you want the facts.
Yes.

May I interject a word in order that we may get our (bearings. I have been greatly interested to learn that nearly every hon. member on the opposite side of the house is opposed' to the Civil Service Commission.
No.
Absolutely the contrary.

I happened to introduce a resolution last year in that connection, and I do not think (there was a single hon. member in the house, with the exception of myself, who spoke in favour of it. The committee was appointed, and where did we get? Just a little bit more trouble is heaped upon the member when he has to go out and scour the country to get someone to take a job which nobody wants. That is about the size of it. If I were to give my opinion of what I thought of the commission, I am afraid it would not be parliamentary.
Try it; you cannot shock this house.

However, like other Conservatives I welcome an advocate such as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough. It is something new for him to stand in this House of Commons and plead for a Tory or a Tory cause. I am sure every hon. member
Supply-Health-Hospitals

on this side of the house, knowing bis ability and knowing how he can argue on any side of a case, will welcome his remarks. But I should like to remind the hon. member that he has made some very quack somersaults in this house. When 'he criticizes the Minister of Pensions and National Health for changing his mind about appointments and at the same time states that the minister should have full liberty to make any appointments he may wish, I suggest lie is inconsistent. I can remember that in a session not very many years ago the hon. member took credit for having a certain vote placed in the estimates. I have no doubt that at the time the vote was in the interests of the good Grits in his riding. But, lo and behold! the next year that very same item was kicked out, and by the very same gentleman. Further, he stood up in this house and on both occasions acknowledged the parentage of it. I wonder if he would now tell us what caused the great conversion in his mind on that occasion, AVhat was the great light which changed him from a Saul to a Paul?
Damascus.

In one year in Lunenburg he pleaded the cause of the Liberals, and as a result had the item placed in the estimates. The next year, simply because they did not bow down and worship him, he returned to this House of Commons, claiming and exercising the right of having the item kicked out of the estimates.
That was consistent.

The hon. member says that is consistent-if inconsistency is consistency yes. On this side of the house we like the hon. member because apparently he is quite frank; generally we know where he stands. But certainly he ought to be a little bit consistent. Hon. members on -this side of the house know what they got when they sat on the opposition benches during the years the Grit government was in power. There was no doubt then as to who exercised the patronage.
You do not know what you are going to get after a while, though.
We will let the future look after itself.
What you are going to get you know not.
We know we could not get a penny postage stamp for our ridings when the Liberals were in power.
Order.

All hon. members on this side recognized that fact in those days. Why not be a little bit consistent? I say that this is not the time for patronage. But if the time ever comes, in my opinion hon. members on this side of the house should have consideration before hon. members opposite.
Regardless of which party may be in power?

Oh, we will be here ; don't worry about that. I do not know why the doctor was dismissed, but the minister has told us that investigations were made. It is not likely that he made the investigations himself, but it is more than likely he appointed competent people to make them- people in whose judgment he had confidence. If he followed their advice I do not believe the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough should be quite so critical. I am sure that had the hon. member been in a similar position he would have been one of the first to follow such advice-and nobody knows it better than he does.

I am sure I appreciate the lecture concerning patronage the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has tried to give me. My hon. friend and I came to this house in 1917. Ever since that time my voice has been raised against the Civil Service Commission, and in favour of the practice of allowing the party in power to make appointments. I never have changed my views in that connection. If the hon. member stated what is in his mind he would admit that I am making a true statement.
Quite true. I merely made the statement that you did not give me any help last year.
I voted for your report.
There was no vote taken.
My hon. friend was a member of the civil service committee, and knowing him as well as I do, when he brought in his report I could do nothing but support him, even though I knew he was wrong.
I was not on the committee, and I never brought in any report.

However, the matter I was discussing before the hon. member spoke is worthy of serious consideration. If I have shown anything, certainly I must have shown the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario that I am trying to be fair. If a Grit doctor had been dismissed and I had objected to the dis-

Supply-Labour
missal, I might understand the hon. member rising in righteous indignation and criticising me. But the fact is that the gentleman I am trying to support and defend is a Conservative.
There must be something wrong when you are defending him.
Putting aside the fact that this good Conservative was dismissed, I should like to ask the minister something about the qualifications of the man who took his place. Were tenders called for or-
Oh, oh!
-or were application forms sent out by the Civil Service Commission?
You are getting too tender altogether.

No, no. Were applications called for by the Civil Service Commission? Did other physicians have an opportunity to apply for this very important position involving the lives of fishermen and sailors, or how was the appointment made?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am responsible for those appointments. I am glad to say there are many medical men in the department. The field is surveyed, and we ascertain who are available and would be suitable. As a result one is chosen and appointed. I cannot say who recommended him, because I have not the files before me. I could not say about most of these appointments, but I satisfied myself to the best of my judgment that this would be a proper appointment.

I quite understand that the minister is willing to take the responsibility, and certainly I do not want to blame him for this appointment. But my hon. friend said he had officials in his department who looked over the field and selected the list from which the appointee was chosen. I should like to know what particular official looked over the field in this case and why this appointment was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Because there was need for it.

I do not think that is a fair answer. They might have gone out and picked a veterinary surgeon, a quack doctor without the necessary qualifications), or a chiropractor or any one. Surely in a case of this kind, where the appointment is important, the minister should be able to give some reason for the choice of this particular gentleman.

I should like to ask a question just to clear up one point in my mind. Did I understand the minister to say that the medical men in these hospitals are appointed not by the Civil Service Commission but by the department directly?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is quite right.
Does that apply to all the hospitals under the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It applies to all the hospitals in the marine section only and port physicians.
It does not apply to the hospitals under the pensions department?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: To nothing else.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: This amount is for the administration of the Annuities Act under which annuities are sold to those who care to invest in them and the contracts are issued by the government.
Can the minister tell us if they are still on the same basis?

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Combines Investigation Act, $25,000.

What investigations
were held last year under this act?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There was an investigation into the Canadian basket pool; there is at present proceeding the coal investigation; there was an investigation into the tobacco industry and there was an investigation last year into the moving picture industry that lapped over into this fiscal year. I have not before me at the moment the details of all the investigations, but I think that covers practically all the investigations during the year.

Is the coal investigation completed as yet?
Supply-Labour

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No. A reference was made in the Senate as to the price of coal in eastern Canada. The situation was drawn to my attention and under the provisions of the act I instructed the registrar, who is the officer charged with such investigations, to proceed with an inquiry. That inquiry is not quite completed; as the hon. member knows this has been a difficult investigation to carry on. About the same time there was an application received in proper form with respect to the mining and sale of coal in western Canada. A preliminary investigation has been made with respect to western Canada, but I have not had a chance to do more than hurriedly review the evidence submitted by our investigators with regard to that situation. Whether or not the evidence we have would justify a further investigation by the registrar I am not able to say at the moment, but the coal inquiry in the east has been going on for some time. I believe the evidence is all in now, and I understand that the report is in course of preparation.
Does not the minister think the investigation should be national while he is at it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The act sets out the method that must be followed in investigations of this character. I think the investigation might be called national if it covers both eastern and western Canada, but whether or not there is sufficient evidence to justify the expense of an inquiry into the mining and sale of coal in western Canada I would not care to say at the moment. I think hon. members will agree that it is not desirable to cause an investigation into private enterprise unless there is at least a prima facie case of something going on in contravention of the terms of the act, because the disturbance of industry by governmental investigations of this kind is not desirable unless such a case is made out. As yet I am not prepared to say that such a case has been made out in western Canada.
When all the evidence in the coal inquiry is in and the minister receives the report will it be made public?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The practice in the past has been I believe not to make these reports public inasmuch as this would necessitate the disclosure of the individual's private business. My own view,' without having looked fully into the past practice, is that if it is determined that further proceedings should follow the report of the registrar in the interests of the public then of necessity that report would have to be made public, being the foundation of such further proceedings as might be deemed

desirable. If however the registrar's report were of such a character that proceedings should end with the reception of it, then, as I think the hon. member will agree with me, it would be highly undesirable to disclose a person's private business to his competitors and to the public.
Were any requests received from British Columbia last year with regard to gasoline prices? I understand that a man named Ormond was refused gasoline by four companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I remember the case to which the hon. gentleman refers. There was a garage man or dealer-
In Victoria.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: In Victoria, yes. He was refused gasoline by some of the wholesalers. The case came under review by the officials of the department and if I remember rightly their report to me was that a case had not been made out such as would justify the registrar making an inquiry. Consequently no further investigation was made.
When will the coal investigation be finished?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It should be through in the course of the next few days. It will take some time to prepare the report based on the evidence but I think it will be ready in its final form before the end of this month.

Mr. HEENAN r Is it the practice of the department now to include in all federal contracts the provisions adopted in 1930 with regard to the eight hour day and fair wages?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Administration, Old Age Pensions Act, $2,000.

I take this opportunity of
presenting to the minister a question in connection with the administration of the act in British Columbia. I reluctantly do it now, having exhausted every other method I know of.
We passed an Old Age Pensions Act, in 1926 I think it was, and the upper house defeated it. We went to the country and it formed a very considerable portion of the discussions on which the election turned. We came back and passed it again the next year, and I think it may be said to have received the very general support of the public throughout Canada. I do not think anyone would seriously propose to repeal it. There are a few reactionaries who think it clever to sneer at it as being socialistic legislation, forgetting that what you spend on the one hand you save on the other, but generally speaking Canada has accepted the spirit of the act.
I will not say that I charge the minister .vith instigating-I want to be as moderate as I can-but by his actions he has encouraged and condoned certain policies being carried out; and whether they had that intention or not the result has been to deprive a large number of deserving people of old age pensions who are fully entitled to them. The local board in British Columbia, acting on instructions-they must have been acting on instructions-suddenly turned a violent right about face. As to the question who gave these instructions, I will deal with that in a moment. They have by every known method of subterfuge and evasion gone directly against both the spirit and the letter of the act in refusing pensions. When I appealed to the minister, as I have done repeatedly-I am going to read the letters-he certainly has encouraged them in their action by ignoring complaints and more or less passing the buck. I have heard him say in this house that the matter is primarily one for the provinces to deal with, or that it was the duty of the provinces. I am inclined to the same view, in
Supply-Labour-Pensions

regard to the original action, but the province of British Columbia specifically and violently denies it. I am going to read the letter of the provincial attorney general on the subject. In any event the minister is responsible for not taking action when it was brought to his attention. It may be said: It is only a case of paying seventy-five per cent of what the province pays out, therefore we have no jurisdiction. That argument will not work. This government is paying out $10,000,000 in this matter; does anyone seriously suggest that the government which pays that $10,000,000 cannot exercise some oversight, cannot say: You are doing this too lavishly, or on too niggardly a scale? Can they not say, I do not think this particular man or woman is entitled to pension? Indeed I have known them to do it, and so they could in respect of an unjustly rejected application. When a case is brought to his attention it is within the scope of the authority and the duty of the minister to draw the attention of the province to the matter and say: Why are you dealing or not dealing with this particular case? It is the same as if I knew of a man in gaol for an offence, and some other person had confessed his guilt and I called that to the attention of the Minister of Justice; it would be his duty, having been apprised of the facts, to take proper action. I do not expect the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Labour to run around the back sections asking people: Have you had a raw deal? But when it is brought to his attention it is his duty to inquire; I will ever maintain that.
As a last resource, I wrote to the Attorney General of British Columbia, and said: "Did you know what was going on?" I thought perhaps it was the board going wrong. This is his reply, dated January 17:
I have your communication of the 13th instant complaining about the administration of the "Old Age Pensions Act."
In the first paragraph of your letter you refer to the provincial old age pensions department. May I state that the provincial government does not administer the Old Age Pensions Act.
That will be news I think for the minister.
This is administered by the Workmen's Compensation Board, it is true, and it is true again that the Workmen's Compensation Board is appointed by the provincial government to administer the "Workmen's Compensation Act," but this board, when administering the "Old Age Pensions Act" is acting for the Dominion government under the dominion statute and pursuant to Dominion government regulations. The board takes its instructions from Ottawa and not from the province.
Please note that.
UVtr. Neill.]
The only change in the system might have been that the Dominion government recently assumed seventy-five per cent of the financial obligations, instead of fifty per cent as was formerly the case.
Who signed that letter?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
What was the date of the letter to which the hon. member received no answer? Was it a letter to me?
Supply-Labour-Pensions

Yes. I think there were five, and later on, after bringing the matter up in the house, I think I got an acknowledgment of three of them. The first letter was dated July 28. I received a sort of blanket acknowledgment from the deputy later on, but not for some months afterward; I shall mention the matter when I come to it. I wrote the minister again on October 26, as follows:
Dear Mr. Gordon:
I would revert to the statement made in my letter to you of July 28 to which I have had no reply. The same situation is still going on, only worse.
The latest case brought to my attention is that of a woman, over seventy, who has been refused a pension although she is sick and over age, on the ground they they consider her husband who is apparently in good physical condition should therefore be able to maintain his wife. The facts are notorious. He is not able to maintain his wife as he cannot get any work, but they refuse the wife's application on the ground that he "should" be able to get work. I submit that that is no answer to the woman's rights under the pension act.
I mentioned a number of other cases in my letter of the date above referred to and suggested that you should have an investigation into the matter. It has got so bad that a lawyer in Victoria has aplied for a mandamus against the provincial official to compel them to grant a pension.
I wrote again on November 3 in regard to another case, and I am citing these because they are all different cases of injustice:
Dear Mr. Gordon:
In reference to the representations I have made to you under date of July 28 and again on October 26 as to the manner in which the Old Age Pensions Act is being administered, I will again call it to your attention with another specific case.
I was not asking him to change the act; I was asking him .to deal with specific cases.
A woman applicant had a property assessed at $3,000. The board insisted on regarding that as its true value although it is a notorious fact that assessments in British Columbia are greatly over-valued. They therefore charged her as if she were getting an income of five per cent on $3,000. Presently she sold it for $2,000 to be paid at the rate of $20 a month, which would naturally take a number of years to complete. The payments were not made very regularly, but on June 1, 1932, the amount due on it was $1,100 to be spread out as I have said at the rate of $20 a month. With the knowledge that the purchaser had defaulted ou several occasions in the past, and that the property was in a small mining town, the board nevertheless took the stand that the property was worth to her $1,100 in cash and that with $1J00 in cash she could buy an annuity of $177 a year. Consequently they charged her up as having that amount of income, which prevented her getting <a pension.
It is a notorious fact that people trying to sell an agreement for the purchase of real

estate have to take a very great discount. A firm in Vancouver, advertising to do such business, said they might have got $800 for this agreement if the property had been situated in Vancouver, but when they heard where it was, they would not touch it at any price, and suggested that I might get a local man to give $400 or $500 for it. It is utterly unfair to say she could purchase an annuity to the equivalent of $1,100 with this agreement of gale because. it will be quite a few years before the amount is received, if then.
One of the regulations says that they must consider the amount of the Canadian government annuity purchasable by the personal property of the pensioner. It is utterly untrue to say that $177 is the amount of the annuity purchasable by this particular piece of property. I would also point out that it is very doubtful whether this should! [be considered personal property. The title to the land is in her name, the agreement of sale has never been registered, and I claim she should only be charged with five per cetot of her interest in the property.
It may be said that this is a provincial matter, but I would point out that your department made an express bargain with the province that they were to grant pensions in ta,ooordanee with the act, and they are not granting pensions in accordance with the act. I submit it is the province of your department to inquire into why they do not.
Another case I will introduce here, and it is the last one, although I could go on for horn's because I have a stack of these oases a couple of feet high. Again I shall not mention the name. A mam was disqualified some years ago because he owned property assessed at such a high figure that at five per cent it produced an assumed income that disqualified him. I pointed out that the property was assessed at five times its true value, being assessed at about $8,000, speaking from memory, while it is worth perhaps $1,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Was that man paying the taxes on the property?
Yes, and keeping himself poor doing it. It was a perfect incubus, a white elephant.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: He should have got rid of that white elephant and saved his taxes.

It takes about three years
to get rid of it by not paying the taxes, and sometimes the government does not hold a tax sale. That was my own recommendation, to let it all go except the house they lived in. I do not know why they did not. But the pension was refused on the ground I have pointed out. Last February the minister's department changed those regulations. The original regulations were that the real estate of a person should be assessed at five per cent of the assessed value. The department found

that that created injustice, probably in Ontario. At any rate they changed the rule, and made it read that in future real estate would be taken at the assessed value, or the market value, whichever was the more equitable. Surely that was a good idea because, after all, we all want equity. As soon as that change was made I applied to the board again and said, "Now I am in a position to get this man a pension because you have been given direct authority, not permission but authority, to take whichever is the more equitable, the assessed or the market value." I offered to show them over the ground so they could see where the property was located, see its poverty and its inability to produce anything at all, and to take their own opinion as to its valuation. What did they do? They said: No, we are going to take the assessed value as being the true value. I pointed out that that was not the true value and that the minister himself had changed his regulations to allow them to take the market value. But they said: No, we are going to take the assessed value.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The regulations read, the
assessed value.

Pardon me, but that was
changed in February a year ago to read, the assessed or market value whichever is the more equitable. I think the minister's deputy will agree with me, and because it was changed in that way this man was entitled to his pension. The board will take a chance today and refuse a pension; using one argument, and a week later they will use the very opposite argument to refuse one if it serves their turn. So they said in this case that they would not take the real market value although the regulations specifically say that they should. So much for that case.
May I add that I received no answer at all to all these letters? As the poet says, there was silence deep as death. But I brought the matter up in the house and made a protest, and next day I got a letter from the minister's deputy, dated November 24, acknowledging receipt of the letters that I had written and saying that "the points raised are being kept in mind for consideration along with a number of other angles which have come to our attention, and I might add to this end the matter of calling a meeting of the interprovincial old age pensions board in the near future is now being considered". But that begs the whole question and evades the point I was asking about. I was not asking the interprovincial board to cal! a meeting. I said:	Tom Jones
and Mrs. Smith have got a raw deal; they are not getting justice; you are the head of the 53719-175
department, and you have the power to give or withhold a pension; it is within your province and authority to deal with that. That was my contention.
At this stage I took the matter up with the Hon. Mr. Pooley, the Attorney General, of British Columbia, with the result I have described. Somehow or other, possibly because it was hard for me to believe that a minister looking so full of benevolence as the Minister of Labour, could lend himself to these cold-blooded acts, I thought I would try once more, hope springing eternal in the human breast.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Is the member referring
to me now?
Yes. Was the minister surprised?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Considerably.

I did not think it possible
that anyone having such an air of genial benevolence could lend himself to such coldblooded acts, and so, Christmas being just over, with its genial spirit, I thought I would try once more. I wrote the minister on January 22, as follows:
Dear Mr. Gordon:
I wrote you three letters last fall on the maladministration of the Old Age Pension Act in British Columbia, citing instances. I had a reply from your deputy to the effect that the points raised would be kept in mind for consideration aDd that a meeting of the interprovincial board might be held.
But I would point out that I was not discussing the general act or its regulations but the flagrant ignoring of the act and overriding it which is being carried on by the provincial administration. I took a specific case up with the provincial attorney general, supposing as the act says and as you yourself have stated in the house, the province was responsible for the administration. The _ provincial attorney general says that the province does not administer the Old Age Pension Act but that you do it through the Workmen's Compensation Board which "takes its instructions from Ottawa and not from the province." This is new doctrine to me and I think untenable. However, if so, it certainly puts it up to you to deal with any specific case of non-compliance with the act. This is not a question of discussing whether the law or the regulations should be changed but of asking you to remedy the grievance of an individual and to give instructions that he be given a pension as entitled under the law. I could cite a score of cases but I am going to deal with a specific one.
Mrs	qualifies in every respect under
the act and the regulations hut has been refused a pension on the ground as stated in their letter now in front of me which reads as follows:
"We note that your husband is not physically incapacitated and that he is under seventy years of age. In view of this it is felt-"

Supply-Labour-Pensions

What business have they to " feel "?' It is the law, not their own petty ideas that should govern:
"-it is felt that he should be in a position to maintain you without receiving assistance from the public treasury. Your application therefore cannot be approved."
Note the suggestion that the woman is asking for charity. She is not asking for charity: she is asking for her rights. Then I go on to say:
They have no right to take this stand. It isn't a question of what they feel this woman should get. Neither the act nor the regulations forbid a woman getting a pension because her husband is under seventy years of age or whether he is able to work or not. The act and the regulations strictly provide how applicant's income shall be calculated and under those regulations she is entitled to a pension because neither she nor her husband are getting any income.
Later on representations were made that the woman was sick and quite unable to travel with her husband in a fishing boat and needed attendance in her home, consequently her husband couldn't even go out and fish. After much pressure the board paid some credence to this and asked a doctor's certificate which was furnished as per attached copy and certainly reveals a serious enough condition, even a non-medical man reading would know she could not go out on a fishing boat for days and nights at a time. You will note that the doctor is very specific about her condition. After receiving it the board advised her that they adhered to their former decision. There are scores of such cases, not similar except in that they refused to grant pensions to people entitled to them, but I submit this specific case to your notice and ask that you deal with it. The Attorney General of British Columbia says the board is under your orders, then I beg you to ask the board why they are not granting this pension. The Pension Act is not permissive but mandatory, if they qualify. No registrar of voters, for instance, would be allowed to refuse a person qualifying under the elections act to be placed on the voters' list because he, the registrar, "felt" that the party did not need a vote or would not make a good use of it.
Now I will quote the certificate of the doctor, and if I have not its terms strictly correct it is because doctors, as we all know, are such bad writers. The certificate is by Dr. 0. O. Lyons, B.A., M.D.C.M., and is dated December 8, 1932.
To whom it may concern:
I have to-day examined Mrs	 She
is suffering from prolapse of the womb, chronic nephritis, hypertension, and gall bladder disease. The hypogastric region is tender due to the gall bladder disease, and this makes it very distressing for her to travel and suffer the jar of a small gas boat. She is quite feeble and should have some one near or in attendance continuously Her condition is not acute and I would not recommend any operative treatment, for her general condition would not permit it.
