One would think that such a letter would produce favourable consideration, but they turned her down. Their reply was: "Your husband1 is under seventy years of age, and he can go out to work." I say the act does not state anything about a woman's husband having to be under seventy years of age. It does say that if anyone is in receipt of an income below a certain sum and comes within the qualifications concerning age and residence, a pension shall be granted.
There is the situation. I have but touched upon the matter; as I say, I could go on for hours citing cases along the lines I have read. Not always the same subterfuge or excuse has been given, but always to the same end. People 'have been turned down-I was going to say if it were humanly possible, but I believe that would be hardly correct. On one occasion I said: "Why do you not do like the wolf about which we read in the story of Little Red Ridinghood? After the little girl had advanced good arguments as to why the wolf should not eat her, the animal lost its patience and said: 'I am going to eat you anyway'." I suggested that they should simply say: "We are going to refuse you, anyway," and not trouble to make excuses. That is the situation -and I have only touched upon, it.
Is it fair and right? WThat is the government going to do about it? It comes home to everybody in the house; responsibility is upon us all. A few years ago there was a Conservative convention in Winnipeg at which that party firmly pledged itself to the extension of the old age pensions scheme. Therefore that party is committed. We come now to the government, every member of which is sworn to administer the laws. How often do we hear it said that no matter how painful the duty may be, a minister has to administer the laws? In case of a strike the militia are turned out. I have heard a minister say: "I am sorry to do it, but I am sworn to administer the laws, and it is my duty so to deal with the matter." In the present instance the same principle applies. I do -not say it is pleasant for them to do so,-but there is the 'law; why do they not administer it? It says in the scriptures: "For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, is guilty of all." I would not go that far, but I would say that if a government is capable of being privy to robbing a poor old .woman of $20 a month, I would not trust them with $2,000,000.
I am sorry the Minister of Justice has left the chamber, but the Minister of Labour is a lawyer. I leave it to any fairminded lawyer; faced with the conditions I have described, would they not carry out the law? Would

Supply-Labour-Pensions
they not go fair to carry out the law? As long as it remained on the statute books it is their duty to carry it out with fairness and equity. The minister says yes?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I have not said anything yet.
I thought you had touched only the edge of it.

There are gentlemen on the government benches-the Minister of National Revenue, and others sitting behind him -big masters of industry, who are heavily concerned in industrial enterprises; what would they think-

The Minister of
National Revenue is not here.
No, he is not there.
Yes, I say he is not there.
Well, I did not say he was present. I referred to anyone on the treasury benches. If he was not there at the moment, that was his funeral.
Hamilton is not all there.
Who is not there?
I never suggested hon. gentlemen opposite were "all" there.

Which is even
better than not being there at all.

Hon. gentlemen are pleased to be humorous, but in my view this is a very serious matter. I was referring to those multimillionaires who are concerned with their fortunes. Supposing our friends to the left, the C.C. F.'ers, as my friend to my right called them, were in power-
Don't let us suppose that; it is absurd. We could not suppose that.
You could not suppose that?
No.
Are you sure.
It is only funny.
Some hon. members opposite are dubious about it, right now.
Don't believe it.

We will suppose some government-without giving it a name-passed a law involving extreme injustice to financial interests which they represented; how quickly they would raise a howl and say: "We want justice." Why not be as quick to ask justice 53719-1751
from this house to remedy an injustice such as I have described? They might look a little bit ahead,-"With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you." If you do not give justice to the poor old men seeking a pension to-day, do not ask us for sympathy if your toes are trod on in years to come.
The Liberal party claims credit for passing old age pension legislation; then certainly they should defend it. The Labour party also claims, with a good deal of sincerity, a great measure of the credit for having passed that legislation. And as the ranks of the old age pensioners are generally-although not always -recruited from the labouring class, they ought to be particularly sensitive about any injustice being done. Then apart from that there is the matter of precedent. If this law is abused, forgotten and ignored, why not others? There are people in Canada, and even in this house, who no doubt would think it a good idea to put the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) in gaol, and keep him there-
We would lose all our fun if we did that.

Such action would not do the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre half the harm that is done to these poor old people. He would receive tremendous advertising through the press; he would soon be out of gaol on a writ of habeas corpus and would suffer no injury. He has been in gaol before, anyway. But we cannot help the poor old woman with a writ of habeas corpus; she is helpless. She has nothing to look forward to but old age and destitution. Then there is this main argument, which must beat a responsive chord in every man's breast, namely the sense of fairness as between man and man, and woman and woman.
That is right.

This is not a matter of popular appeal. I have no press behind me. There are no great financial interests involved; they will not worry much about the old woman's position. No columnist will be able to write a snappy article about the drab dreary record of a poor old woman's efforts to live on a couple of dollars a month. You cannot make snappy copy out of that. In the very nature of things, these people are poor, financially down and out, unknown in public, private or political life. "There are only a few thousand of them-why bother? Their votes won't amount to much in a public way, anyway. Why bother about them?" Well, they belong to the same class as they about whom it was once said, "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto
Supply-Labour-Pensions

one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto Me." At least they belong to that class. Perhaps in the sight of the Ruler of the Universe they are just as important as any king, knight, prince, premier or any of the rest of us.
I am not given to suggesting a filibuster or obstruction, but if I had six supporters in this house I would guarantee that not a cent of money in supply would be voted until this wrong had been righted. That is what supply is for; that is why we are here. I would not consent to supply until at least I had a promise-
We would be here all year if there were six like you.

I am sorry I did not hear the hon. member's remark, but I recall it is said that the fresher the fish is, the better and more beautiful the fish. Of course that does not apply to the hon. member. It only puts him into the poor fish class, when he sees fit to make such interruptions.
A pretty stale old fish, I tell you.

Quite so.
I place the responsibility on the house, on the government and on each individual member thereof. As to how they discharge that responsibility they will have to answer at the bar of public opinion at the next election, and possibly also at the bar of a higher court, the summons to which is inevitably drawing nearer for us all.
Now I want to ask the Minister of Labour specifically whether he endorses the statement of the Attorney General of British Columbia that his department is giving instructions to this board in that province. Whether t'he minister's reply is yes or no I want to ask him if he does not realize his responsibility as the supervisor of this large sum of federal money which is contributed, and whether he cannot and will not insist on justice being done. I shall be very glad to furnish the minister with the fullest details of these specific cases, names and everything, and I would beg him on bended knee, if that would be any good, to remedy the conditions which exist. I will be his henchman for ever and ever if he will do justice to these poor people.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I am sure I appreciate the feelings of the hon. member when, during the course of his activities in his own province or elsewhere, he sees some human who is not enjoying as comfortable an old age as the ordinary person perhaps feels he is entitled to enjoy. It is a difficult situation; it is one of

those complexities of human life that we have encountered since history began and which I presume will continue to the end. No one sympathizes with the hon. member more than I do; I am sure that when he sees such conditions as he has described it does not give him any sense of satisfaction.
With respect to the act itself, it is a dominion statute passed by this chamber for the purpose of providing the money to pay a proportion of an old age pension to those who come under the provisions of the act and the regulations in connection with it. For reasons upon which I need not enlarge our share is in the nature of a contribution; the fund is administered by the provinces, and the act itself is administered through the agency of the provinces. The agreement is entered into with the provinces, and the regulations are submitted to the provincial authorities. The act contemplates that these regulations ^hall prevail for a certain number of years. The regulations, it is true, have been varied from time to time, and were changed but a short year or so ago.
This is social legislation of a kind that all countries have not adopted. All countries do not see the force of the principle that underlies this measure. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni in his suggestion that there is not a direct responsibility upon the sons and the daughters to see that their aged parents receive that support to which they are entitled. I never have been able to bring myself to view with indifference the thought of children in positions of affluence or comfortably well to do who aTe permitted to take the attitude that they do not owe a responsibility to their parents far greater than any responsibility the state may owe. If we permit an undisciplined administration of this or any other act, thereby relieving those who are primarily responsible for the care of their immediate blood relatives, then I feel confident that we are not going along the path we should follow, because it will not be long until there will be no feeling of responsibility on the part of the children to contribute to the care of their parents in a large number of cases. To encourage the younger people of this or any other country whose aged parents are alive to follow that line of thought is something that will not help in the future and will not tend to build up that class of society I want to see in this country.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say it was a proper thing for the provinces to pass acts similar to that to which reference has been made, under which children who are able to contribute to the support of their parents and refuse to do so will find the law set in motion

Supply-Labour-Pensions
to force them to do their duty. I believe that is proper and sane legislation. On the other hand I say that any of these acts that tends to take care of those who happen upon misadventure or who are entering the twilight of their lives without adequate support should not destroy that sense of responsibility, of respect, of love and affection that the child should bear towards his parents.
With respect to the province of British Columbia, it is obvious that as Minister of Labour I cannot inquire into individual cases; I think hon. members will readily realize that it would be utterly impossible for me to do so.
Why not, in a specific case?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I am coming to that in a moment. When a complaint does come to the department that those administering this act in any province are perhaps not administering it as the law and the regulations contemplate, then it is the practice of the department-and I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member for Comox-Alberni say that the practice was not followed in his cases-to direct the attention of the provincial authorities to the case in question, asking them to investigate it and determine to what extent the complaint is well founded. After this item passes I should be very glad indeed if the hon. member would give me a list of the letters he has written to which he says he has had no reply, with their dates and the names of the cases, and I can assure him that I will have them investigated and a report furnished me in order to see to what extent, if any, the law and the regulations have not been enforced in British Columbia.
In order that hon. members may not judge the province of British Columbia only in the light of these cases to which reference has been made by the hon. member I think it desirable to give some figures. In the province of British Columbia the percentage of pensioners to the population over seventy years of age, actually receiving pensions under this act, is 50-72. Compare that with the province of Ontario, for instance, where the percentage is only 34-62. Having that general picture before us we will see that generally throughout the province of British Columbia there must have been a very generous interpretation of the act and the regulations with respect to those aged people who fall within the provisions of the act. That is as far as I can go with regard to the figures.
Has the minister the figures for Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Alberta, 51.20, about the same as British Columbia, and Ontario, 34.62. Ontario, I may say, has the law to which I made reference with respect to the necessity of children contributing to the care of their parents. I do not know that I can add anything more to what I have said. The province certainly sets up the machinery to administer old age pensions, and if the interpretation of Mr. Pooley's letter is that they do not administer the act, then I very respectfully suggest that that gentleman has misconstrued the position with respect thereto. The machinery in British Columbia I am told is operated through the agency of the Workmen's Compensation Board and unless there is something radically wrong with the set-up of that board I doubt whether there are people better able to determine who should or should not receive old age pensions, having regard to the experience of the board in workmen's compensation cases. I do not want to be unfair to those who are administering the affairs of the provinces, because they have great and difficult problems to face; but there are bound to be some instances in the administration of an act of this sort where it might appear that through one cause or another, or through a combination of causes, there has been a hardship, that someone has not been given that consideration to which his case entitles him. I can only repeat that if the hon. member will supply me with the dates of his letters and the name of the applicant, the department, on my instructions, will investigate as I have indicated and see that justice is done, if it is found that there has been injustice in the premises.

I am much indebted to the minister; what he says shows that my faith in his benevolence is not altogether unfounded. I am glad to hear him say that he will investigate these eases and I am quite satisfied to abide by his decision. He will find that they are as I have stated and that injustice has been done. Indeed, the situation is so bad that a lawyer in Victoria, acting probably without recompense, took up a case and entered a mandamus against the officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Did he succeed?
It was thrown out of the first court on a technicality, on the ground that he should have proceeded not by mandamus but by fiat, and in the second court it was thrown out on a similar technicality.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
He never got to first base with his case.
Supply-Labour-Pensions

The thing has got to be so notorious that a society has been formed in Vancouver-there is nothing to be gained by it personally, so far as any member of the society is concerned-to try to have justice done these people.
I want to comment on one or two points made by the minister, wherein in my opinion he was not quite fair. He quoted the percentage of people over seventy in British Columbia as 50.72, and this he said showed that they must have been treated very generously in that province. Well, you can always prove anything by figures, but I submit that the figure quoted by the minister does not show the conclusion which he reached. What it does show is that there are more elderly people, especially bachelors, in British Columbia than young peojfie, and that makes the percentage of those over seventy years of age greater.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: More than in Ontario?

Yes. There are not as many young married people in British Columbia but far more elderly people, bachelors particularly, and it is well known that all the cranks drift west and stop there. I am myself an instance. The minister also said that he hoped it was not due to the personnel of the board. No; the personnel of the board are all right; I know them personally. But if their instructions are wrong-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: They must follow the regulations.

I sincerely wish they would
follow the regulations, but it is then- secret instructions that are wrong. If they would follow the regulations as I have outlined them, although I do not approve of some of the regulations the minister made last February, old people would generally be able to obtain pensions under reasonable conditions.
The minister dealt with the Parents' Maintenance Act and he took the sound standard ground that a man certainly should be held to take care of his parents if he is able to. But I am not dealing with cases where children are able to take care of their parents; I am referring to those who are not able to do so. Can it be said that a man receiving $5.60 a month on relief is capable of supporting his parents? I asked the province to administer the Old Age Pensions Act on the face of it, so to speak, and if they thought that the children were wealthy and able to pay their share then the province could sue. The province has the authority and the

money, and a poor old man or woman should not be placed in the humiliating position of having to sue his or her children when they know that the children would be quite willing to help if they could.
I deprecate the attitude taken by the board when they say, "You are asking for charity and we feel that you should not become a public charge". But I submit it is not public charity; it is a public right. These people have as much right to receive a pension if they qualify as I have the right to vote if I have the qualifications. I shall be glad to furnish the minister with the information he asks for and if he deals with these cases it will perhaps lead to a better interpretation of the act in British Columbia in the future.

I would direct to the
attention of the minister one particular case with regard to which I have had correspondence, though not with this department. A man has lived thirty years or more in Canada and is eligible in every way for old age pension, except in this regard, that during the last five years he has lived three years in Saskatchewan and two in Alberta. When he writes to Alberta they say he has not been five years in that province and that therefore they cannot do anything; he writes to Saskatchewan and they say he has not been resident five years there and so they cannot do anything either. I understand that there is an arrangement among the provinces that if a period of twenty years has been spent partly in one province and partly in another they will divide the costs, but apparently there is no such arrangement with respect to the last five years. Will the minister let us know whether there is a possibility of a man in such a situation getting a pension. It so often happens that people living close to the border between two provinces move from one province to the other and thus are at a great disadvantage.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The question raised by the hon. member was given consideration at the provincial conference. I have the matter now before me and there is no doubt about it, if the principle of the legislation itself is sound, that there is what would appear to be the exclusion of a certain class by reason of provincial boundary lines. However, I hope that the difficulty will be determined by agreement.

One phase of the question raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has been brought to my notice and it does seem to me to show a rather harsh interpretation of the law. I refer to the case

Supply-Labour-Pensions
where the aged person owns certain property which is non-revenue-producing and which still may be assessed at a fair figure. I might cite one case by way of illustration of this point. It is a man of eighty-six who put in forty-five years in my district farming. He came there from the old country, one of the fine type of old English farmers. He worked hard and did fairly well. Unfortunately he was of generous instincts, although a York-shireman, and the little money he made he loaned on mortgage to certain of his neighbours who, being farmers, are utterly unable at this time to pay a cent of principal or interest. He still has the old quarter-section, and manages to have it farmed and to get out of it just about enough to pay the taxes on it. But in applying for old age pension- and he ha.s paid taxes for forty-five years-he forgets that phase of the regulations; the department have taken an estimate of all his property, have placed a fairly high assessment on it, and assume that he is getting or should get five per cent on that amount. The fact is that for six years to my knowledge he has not received $2 on it, nevertheless he is down in their books as receiving an estimated income of five per cent on that property. He is perfectly willing to turn the property over to the department, and to sign a quit claim giving them the right of collection so that if anything comes in later they will get it. But in the meantime he has to live, and he is being refused pension on that ground; although, as I have said, there is no income from that property, it is assumed that he is getting five per cent on the assessed value of it. I think that is rather a harsh provision, and I would like to have it looked into. By the way, although the man is an Alberta man it was the British Columbia government that made that ruling.

I was just
going to speak about the same matter but from a different aspect. I came across several cases in our province last year, which I think indicates one reason why the percentages are swelled somewhat, in which parents who had children in comfortable circumstances and who owned property, apparently under some provision of the act are able to turn the property over to the department and receive a pension. I know three such individuals who in my estimation could not qualify for old age pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
They do not turn their
property over to this department.

No, I mean to the authorities in the province, and they, I assume, administer the property. I cannot understand why the same procedure was not
adopted in the case mentioned by my hon. friend from Red Deer. The thought that occurred to me was that rather than being stringent there was considerable leniency exhibited in the administration of the act; for frankly I could not see why these persons should receive old age pension, why they should not carry on with their own property and live on the receipts. In one case particularly both husband and wife are in receipt of $20 a month each. No cases of hardship have come to my notice, but those cases caused me some surprise to find the act was interpreted so generously. The case mentioned by my hon. friend would come within the same category.
Mr. SPEAKMAN; The hon. member asks why the old man did not live on the receipts from his property. I stated that there were no receipts of any kind, but that it was assumed by the department that there were.

I was pleased to hear the
minister's remark regarding transients. Numerous cases with .regard to old age pensions have been brought to my attention, and I am going to cite one which was referred to me since I came to Ottawa, that of a woman of Canadian birth resident four years in British Columbia and sixteen years in Saskatchewan. British Columbia said: You have not been here long enough. She wrote to Saskatchewan; Saskatchewan paid no attention. I took it up with the Saskatchewan department but I have heard nothing from them. The minister says it is a provincial regulation, but I think there should be some dominion control in regard to such cases. I suppose Saskatchewan takes the view that these people having left the province, they need pay no attention to them. The act needs tightening up in that regard. I would ask the minister what he would do with regard to people who, having resided in another province for many years, move into British Columbia but are not there long enough to come under the British Columbia act.

I believe the old people
of British Columbia owe a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni for the very excellent case he has made in regard to getting the administration of this act improved. I was privileged to see much of the correspondence that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni had in regard to this matter. A good many cases of somewhat the same character have been brought to my attention. One man lived in British Columbia thirty-five years, brought up his family there, and now finds himself without any means. He was in every way entitled to pension under the
Supply-Labour-Pensions

Old Age Pensions Act, but when he made application they told him he could not qualify because he had adult children living in the province. Apart from the fact that some of his sons were out of employment, I think as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has said it is asking too much to expect a parent to prosecute his son for lack of maintenance. If prosecution of that kind has to be undertaken, those administering the act should do the dirty work. The minister made reference to the duty of children to look after their parents when they come to an age when they are not capable of looking after themselves. That really is rather strange. I have heard biblical authority quoted in this house for many things; may I give one quotation on this point? I think it was St. Paul who said that it. was not for children to make provision for their parents, but for parents to make provision for their children. In any case I think that is fairly good philosophy.
The other point that I wish to make is in regard to the interpretation of the act in British Columbia. The minister quoted the percentage of old people receiving pensions in that province, suggesting that it showed the administration had not been unduly restrictive. I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni answered that very well. It must be remembered that British Columbia was the first province to come under the act, and for that reason would have more people receiving old age pensions than a province that came in later.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That would not have any bearing upon it.

It would have a great
deal, because a province that has been under the act only six months would not have as many as one that has been under it a much longer period.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
It applies to everyone
within the age.

Quite so. We have other pension legislation in this country; does anyone suggest that some other act should be invoked to do these people out of their pensions? Would we suggest that because a judge has children who should be able to keep him, he should not get his pension? Why can we not apply the same measure to old people who because of poverty come under the old age pensions legislation, as we apply in the case of judges who for many years before their retirement received good salaries? Moreover, on some cases they are drawing other 
salaries in addition to their pensions. It is time we should deal more fairly with the old people who are not able to do anything for themselves.

Along with the hon.
member for Kenora-Rainy River, I had the honour of signing the agreement that brought old age pensions into force in Ontario. The members of the labour movement have always felt that this should be an old age pension act, providing a pension to be paid to the aged people for services rendered to the state and to the community. Mention has been made of the Parents' Maintenance Act. The minister says that the law should be set in motion to place the responsibility on the children, but the law is not set in motion. In Ontario the Parents' Maintenance Act was a dead letter until the passage of the Old Age Pensions Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: WThat does the hon. member mean by that?
Well, it was not used.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I do not think the hon.
member is correct in that.

I am speaking in a
broad way. It is not used even to-day. I do not think there will be any contradiction of that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Well, I contradict it.

I believe the responsibility should rest upon the province. I want to qualify that by this statement, that I do not think it is anybody's business what the income of the old person is. The pension should be treated purely as one paid to the old people, as I said before, for the contribution they have made in building up this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Whether they need it or
not?

That is not the ques-
'ion. If they do not need it, they do not lave to apply for it. But as the hon. mem-)er for Vancouver South said, in relation to *he expenditure of the country, it stands in ;he same position as the pension of a judge who is paid one for the contribution he has made to the state. I am glad the minister cleared up the question with regard to the responsibility for administration of the act. From the remarks of and the letters read by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I felt that the federal government at least had given instructions in connection with the regulations and that the responsibility was

Supply-Labour-Pensions
taken away from the provinces and now rested entirely with the federal authorities. Had the federal government accepted the full responsibility for the payment of old age pensions, in accordance with the policy enunciated by them at the last federal election, it is fair to assume the whole administration of old age pension legislation would have to be taken over by the federal authorities.
There is a great deal to be said in connection with the residence provision. Before an applicant for a pension comes within the jurisdiction of the legislation five years' residence in a province is required. Supposing an old person lived in Manitoba for thirty years and then moved into Ontario, it is unfair that he should be disqualified from receiving a pension. That is a point which might well be taken into consideration by the government. But I want to reiterate, so far as Ontario is concerned, that the provincial commission has not proceeded under the Parents' Maintenance Act; it has just taken it for granted that the children can make some contribution to the maintenance of their parents. I am not going to weary the house by quoting many cases I could cite, but the fact remains that in many instances pensions have been reduced where, in my judgment, there has been absolutely no justification when one considers the income received by the children themselves.

The hon. member for East Hamilton put his finger on a very delicate subject when he said that he thought the federal government ought to take over in its entirety the administration of the old age pensions scheme. I am satisfied that the people of Canada are looking for the federal government to carry out its pledge in that regard. I am also satisfied there would be more complaints along the lines of those which have been brought up by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, were it not for the fact that the people of Canada are waiting, before this parliament dissolves, for the federal government to carry out its pledge and to take over the old age pension plan as a national obligation. In the meantime I think the minister will find that many of these grievances arise out of the fact that the provincial governments are complicating the matter by mixing up two statutes, the Old Age Pensions Act and the Parents' Maintenance Act.
The Old Age Pensions Act, as enacted in 1927, is very clear and specific, in that it provides a pension for a person who is a British subject and is not in receipt of an income of as much as $365 a year. It does
not say: "Provided the children cannot maintain their parents." It is true the Parents' Maintenance Act in the provinces contains that provision, but the Old Age Pensions Act that we have on the statute book of Canada provides that if a person is not in receipt of an income of $365 a year, he is entitled to an old age pension. Where the provinces come in is that they suggest that, notwithstanding the fact that a person is entitled to a pension under the old age pension plan, they can invoke the power vested in them by the Parents' Maintenance Act. I contend that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is right when he sas^s that the old people should receive the pension as provided under the Old Age Pensions Act and then, if the provinces have any rights in the matter under the Parents' Maintenance Act, they should sue the children under that act. But in no case does the Parents' Maintenance Act of a provincial legislature have any right to prohibit the payment of a pension under the Old Age Pensions Act.
With regard to the question brought up by the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Medicine Hat with respect to the five years' residence, I may say for the information of the minister, who was not in the house in 1927 when we enacted this law, that for the protection of British Columbia the five year residence provision was at that time inserted in the act. British Columbia was the first province that signified its willingness to come in under the act, and we realized that if only one province came in there would be a rush of older people from the rest of the country into British Columbia. So we inserted the five year residence provision in order to protect that province. The day for the need of that protection has gone by. Five provinces are now participating in the old age pension pl^n, and I am satisfied that the provinces would be quite willing to eliminate that five year residence provision, or leave it at one year if there is necessity for such a provision. I would urge the minister to give con-iderntiion to that question, because I know that before I left office the five provinces were quite willing that the five year residence provision should be eliminated from the act. I would ask the minister if there are now any more provinces participating in the old age pension plan than there were in 1930, and how many old age pensioners there are at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
At the present time the
provinces which have adopted the old age pension scheme are Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. The
Supply-Labour-Pensions

other provinces have not. The question of the five years' residence, of course, has been the subject matter of discussion and debate; at least, I saw some fragmentary references to it over the past few years in the files of the Labour department. There is the danger that aged people will cross the border of a province that is not under the act into a province that is, and the province that happens to be under the act will suffer acordingly a severe burden.
With respect to the administration of the act generally, while I cannot deny that there may be, and probably are, individual cases of hardship where perhaps the province in its administration of the act, or its officials, have not conformed strictly to the act or to the agreements and regulations, yet the volume of opinion which I have had the opportunity to review is that the act generally is being administered very generously. In fact, as was pointed out by the hon. member for West Edmonton, the officers administering the act apparently have rather tortured the regulations in order to bring people within its scope. I will bear in mind what the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has said, and see what can be done. Answering his last question, the total number of pensioners as of December 31, 1932, was 70,516.

Can the minister give us
any information with respect to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, both of which provinces in 1928 I think passed acts enabling them to make agreements with the Dominion government, which acts were not to come into effect except on proclamation?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That proclamation has not yet been issued.

Does the minister know
any reason why?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No.

Can the minister tell us
whether or not this government intends bringing into effect a national system of old age pensions and administering it federally?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Of course, constitutional
questions might arise between the Dominion government and the provinces if the Dominion government adopted that course. At the moment I am not in a position to answer that question.

Has the government made
any estimate of how much it would cost this government to pay old age pensions all over the Dominion of Canada out of the federal treasury?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
That would depend in
large measure upon the number of those eligible by reason of age who took advantage of the legislation. I am afraid it would be difficult to hazard an opinion as to what it would cost.
No estimate has been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I am told that there was
an estimate made in so faa- as it could be made. Unfortunately I have not the figures before me, but I shall be glad to give them to my hon. friend.

I am asking now for the figures. I should not think it would be very difficult to make an approximate estimate of the cost. The government could take its experience in the provinces which have adopted old age pensions and make the necessary allowance for the increased number of those [DOT] over seventy years of age in the eastern provinces-because I believe there is an increased number there-and in that way arrive at an estimate of the cost. I was wondering if the government had not done that. I say that because, as the minister probably knows, this was one of the live questions in Nova Scotia in the election of 1930. I do not suppose there was any canvass that was responsible for getting more votes for the 'Conservative party in Nova Scotia than the definite promise to pay old age pensions in full out of the federal treasury. Those of us who went through that election have a vivid recollection of the strength of the canvass that was made against us because we were supporting a policy of a fifty-fifty contribution as against a policy of one hundred per cent contribution out of the federal treasury. The Prime Minister himself wrote a letter which went to a very large proportion of the aged people in Nova Scotia in which he definitely promised that if returned to power his government would see that old age pensions would >be paid in full out of the federal treasury. But the government has not done it, and so far as I know they have not any present intention of doing it.
Another broken promise.
It appears to be and was a cold-blooded violation of an exceedingly definite preelection promise.
Did the people believe them?

Yes, a great many of them voted that way on the strength of that promise. If possible I should like to get from the minister such an estimate, if one has been made. I should also like him to tell me, if

Supply-Labour-Pensions
he can, whether the government have abandoned that policy, or whether they have any intention of carrying it out some time, and if so, when.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into the question of the estimate and send the hon. member any figures which are available in the department on the subject.
What about the preelection promise?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I never make any promises as to the future.

The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked the minister the same question, whether the government has any intention of carrying out that preelection promise of 1930. Has the government any intention of carrying it out?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I am not in a position at the moment to answer that question.
I think, Mr. Chairman, the minister ought to answer the question more seriously.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I was never more serious in my life.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that you coming from Nova Scotia do not want this item carried until we get that information because you are aware that no people were ever deceived so much as were the people of Nova Scotia in the last election on this question. I was down there during the election and I could not hear anything else but the Conservative candidates promising a federal system of old age pensions, and the Prime Minister himself iterated and reiterated that policy from every platform from one end of Canada to the other. The government has now been in office for nearly three years and nothing has been done to carry out that promise. I do not think the minister should get away with simply saying that he cannot state whether the government is going to do it or not.
What about your promises to the soldiers of a gratuity for everyone in 1921?

Will any member of the government say that they did not promise a national system of old age pensions in 1930? Even in the Conservative platform of 1927 the words, as I recall them, were that the old age pension system as at present existing was
unworkable and inadequate, and the Conservative platform called for a national system of old age pensions. During the last election the Prime Minister and his colleagues and his candidates from one end of the country to the other, but particularly down in Nova Scotia, where the people were not receiving old age pensions at all, made a very definite promise. I recall very well the pledge of the present Minister of Finance. Surely we ought to have an answer from the minister with whose estimates we are now dealing. If they are not going to do it, we ought to know it; if they are considering it, we ought to know it; if they are going to do it, the minister ought to make an announcement. They ought to be proud to state that is one pledge they intend to carry out. I do not believe the minister should treat the matter as lightly as he seems to treat it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

speechtext: You are too good to stay in politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I do know about a lot of promises made in the Liberal manifesto of 1919 which were not kept. I have no doubt that in some instances efforts were made to keep them, but there was a wholesale disregard of others. Undoubtedly they were but pious hopes. Perhaps one might say that it is a poor man who cannot make a promise.
Progress reported.
